tiles.label: Federal aid suspended — winnable with appeal
tiles.spokenText: Federal aid suspended — winnable with appeal

tiles.label: SAP appeals usually win
tiles.subtitle: But the deadline is tight
tiles.spokenText: If you have been notified that you lost federal financial aid because of Satisfactory Academic Progress — SAP — the appeal process exists exactly for this reason. A complete, well-documented appeal that names a recognized circumstance and shows a plan to regain SAP has the strongest chance. The deadline is usually short — often within fourteen days of the notice, though it varies by school. Start TODAY and ask financial aid for the exact deadline at this school.

tiles.label: Read the notice
tiles.subtitle: Which standard failed?
tiles.spokenText: Read your SAP-failure notice carefully. Federal SAP has three standards: GPA (usually 2.0 minimum), pace of completion (usually 67 percent of attempted credits earned), and maximum time frame (usually 150 percent of program length). The notice should tell you which one you failed. Different standards have different appeal arguments.

tiles.label: Document your specific circumstance
tiles.subtitle: 34 CFR 668.34
tiles.spokenText: Federal regulation 34 CFR section 668-point-34 names specific bases for an SAP appeal: the death of a relative of the student, an injury or illness of the student, or other special circumstances. Document yours: medical records, death certificate, mental-health provider letter, police report for DV, financial documentation. The school sets its own appeal procedures within this framework.

tiles.label: Gather documentation
tiles.subtitle: Doctor / dean / counselor letters
tiles.spokenText: Gather: medical records or doctor letter for illness, death certificate for bereavement, counselor or therapist letter for mental health, police report for DV, FAFSA or other docs for financial hardship, advisor letter explaining the academic struggle, your own statement. The more concrete the documentation, the stronger the appeal.

tiles.label: Plan to get back to SAP
tiles.subtitle: Required for appeal
tiles.spokenText: Federal regulations require your appeal to include a plan to regain SAP — usually within one to three terms. Work with your academic advisor to build a realistic plan: which classes, what GPA per term, what supports you will use. Include this in your written appeal. Show that you have a path forward, not just an explanation of the past.

tiles.label: If appeal granted — probation
tiles.subtitle: One-term grace
tiles.spokenText: If your appeal is granted, you will usually be placed on Financial Aid Probation for one term. During probation you keep your aid but must meet the academic plan. Hit the plan and you go back to good standing. Miss it and you lose aid again.

tiles.label: Appeal denied — second appeal?
tiles.subtitle: Limited but possible
tiles.spokenText: If your appeal is denied, ask the financial aid office: is there a second-level appeal? Can I submit additional documentation? Some schools allow a second appeal with new evidence. If not, you may be able to pay out of pocket for one term, raise your GPA / completion rate, and regain SAP for the following term without aid.

tiles.label: Can't pay — emergency funds
tiles.subtitle: Bridge to next term
tiles.spokenText: If your appeal was denied and you cannot pay out of pocket for the next term, the Dean of Students office often has emergency grants. Some institutions have institutional aid that is separate from federal aid. Outside scholarships are another bridge.

tiles.label: Medical reason — also drop / withdraw
tiles.subtitle: Coordinate paths
tiles.spokenText: If your SAP failure was due to medical reasons, also consider whether a medical withdrawal from the failed term — backdated through the dean of students — could be cleaner than the appeal. Sometimes a medical withdrawal followed by re-enrollment in a future term has better aid implications than an appeal-with-probation.

tiles.label: Veteran benefits + SAP
tiles.subtitle: Different rules
tiles.spokenText: If you receive Post-9/11 GI Bill or other veteran benefits, SAP rules and appeals are slightly different — VA has its own. Talk to your campus Veterans Services office in addition to financial aid.

tiles.label: Routine housing requests
tiles.spokenText: Routine housing requests

tiles.label: Roommate conflict (not crisis)
tiles.subtitle: Dishes · sleep · guests
tiles.spokenText: Routine roommate conflict — like dishes, sleep schedules, music, guests. The first step is usually a roommate-agreement conversation, often mediated by your Resident Assistant. The RA can also help you draft a roommate agreement document, which makes future conflicts easier to resolve. If conflict escalates beyond routine, the Resident Director gets involved.

tiles.label: Roommate crisis (sexual / substance / MH)
tiles.subtitle: Different path
tiles.spokenText: If the roommate situation is more serious — sexual harassment, substance abuse endangering me, mental-health crisis — the kiosk has a separate roommate-crisis path with safer options.

tiles.label: Maintenance request
tiles.subtitle: Heat · plumbing · pests
tiles.spokenText: For maintenance issues in your dorm room — heat / cooling, plumbing leak, broken window, pest sighting — submit a maintenance request through the residence-life portal. For urgent issues (no heat in winter, water leak, mold) call the residence-life on-call line for same-day response.

tiles.label: Locked out
tiles.subtitle: RA / RD on-call
tiles.spokenText: For dorm lockout, contact your Resident Assistant first. They can let you in or page the on-call Resident Director. Many campuses charge a small fee for after-hours lockouts; the first one is often waived.

tiles.label: Lost or stolen key / card
tiles.subtitle: Replace at One Card
tiles.spokenText: For lost or stolen room key or campus ID card, go to the OneCard or campus ID office to replace it. Some campuses also let you self-suspend a lost ID online to prevent unauthorized use until you can get to the office. Bring photo ID.

tiles.label: Move-in / move-out logistics
tiles.subtitle: Dates · keys · check-out
tiles.spokenText: For move-in or move-out — assigned dates, key pickup/return procedure, room inspection process, mail forwarding, storage between semesters — your Residence Life office has the official move-in and move-out guides.

tiles.label: Summer storage
tiles.subtitle: On + off campus options
tiles.spokenText: For storing belongings between semesters: some campuses provide free on-campus storage in unused spaces, especially for international students who cannot fly with everything. Storage Squad and Dorm Room Movers are common off-campus options used by college students nationwide. Ask Residence Life for the campus storage policy.

tiles.label: Emotional support animal
tiles.subtitle: ESA accommodation
tiles.spokenText: For an emotional support animal in a dorm: this is a disability accommodation request. Many campuses route ESA requests through Disability Services, but some use Housing or a housing portal first — check your campus housing portal or Disability Services to find out which applies. You will need a letter from a treating mental-health provider. Submit early — the process takes a few weeks. ESAs are not service animals; the rules and rights are different.

tiles.label: Parking, towing, bike, shuttle
tiles.spokenText: Parking, towing, bike, shuttle

tiles.label: Parking permit
tiles.subtitle: Apply or renew
tiles.spokenText: For a campus parking permit — apply through your campus parking-services office. Most campuses have student / commuter / resident / faculty-staff tiers with different prices. Permits are usually annual; some campuses let you pay by semester.

tiles.label: Parking citation — appeal
tiles.subtitle: Tight deadline
tiles.spokenText: For a parking citation appeal — appeal windows are short and campus-specific, so check the citation itself or the parking-services portal immediately. Submit through the parking-services website. Common winning arguments: signage was obscured, vehicle was disabled, you had a valid permit displayed but it was missed.

tiles.label: My car was TOWED
tiles.subtitle: Find it + retrieve
tiles.spokenText: If your car was towed from campus — call parking-services first to find out which tow company has it and where the lot is. Bring registration, insurance, and ID. Tow fees and storage fees grow daily — go as soon as possible.

tiles.label: Bike registration
tiles.subtitle: Theft protection
tiles.spokenText: For free bike registration — most campuses register bikes through campus police. They take the serial number plus your contact info. Registered bikes are much more likely to be recovered if stolen, and the campus has a way to identify abandoned bikes vs registered ones.

tiles.label: Bike was STOLEN
tiles.subtitle: Police report
tiles.spokenText: For a stolen bike — file a campus police report immediately. The kiosk will route you to the police-report wizard, which covers theft and other property reports in addition to safety incidents. Bring the serial number if you registered, or any photos that show identifying features. Check the campus abandoned-bike lot a few days later — sometimes thieves abandon bikes once they realize they cannot use them.

tiles.label: Campus shuttle
tiles.subtitle: Routes + accessibility
tiles.spokenText: For campus shuttle schedules, accessibility shuttles, and route maps — most campuses publish these on the transportation-services website. Ask the front desk for the printed schedule if you cannot find the website. Many shuttles are free for students with a campus ID.

tiles.label: Late-night safety escort
tiles.subtitle: Walk + ride
tiles.spokenText: For a late-night safety escort — most campuses offer free walking escorts or shuttle pickups for students traveling alone late at night. Call campus police or campus safety. This is not just for emergencies — you can request one any time you feel unsafe walking alone.

tiles.label: UConn Police Department
tiles.subtitle: 126 North Eagleville Road · 860-486-4800
tiles.spokenText: UConn Police Department. Address: 126 North Eagleville Road, Storrs, CT 06269. Phone: 860-486-4800.

tiles.label: Password, wifi, devices, software
tiles.spokenText: Password, wifi, devices, software

tiles.label: Password reset
tiles.subtitle: Self-serve usually
tiles.spokenText: For a password reset — most campuses have a self-serve password reset link from the login page. If self-serve does not work, call the IT help desk. Bring your campus ID — they will verify before resetting in person.

tiles.label: Account is LOCKED
tiles.subtitle: Multiple wrong attempts
tiles.spokenText: If your account is locked after multiple wrong-password attempts, the IT help desk can unlock it. Some campuses auto-clear lockouts after a wait, but timing varies — stop retrying (more attempts may extend the lockout) and contact the IT help desk.

tiles.label: Two-factor authentication problem
tiles.subtitle: Lost phone / no signal
tiles.spokenText: For two-factor authentication problems — lost phone, no cell signal, new phone — the IT help desk can issue temporary backup codes or reset your 2FA enrollment. Most campuses use Duo or Microsoft Authenticator; both have offline backup-code options you can set up in advance.

tiles.label: Wifi access
tiles.subtitle: Guest or student
tiles.spokenText: For campus wifi — your campus ID and password should log you in to the student wifi automatically. For guest wifi (visitors, parents), most campuses have a separate guest network with a short registration. Eduroam is the international academic wifi network that works on many campuses worldwide if you have credentials from your own school.

tiles.label: Stolen laptop
tiles.subtitle: Report + lock + report
tiles.spokenText: For a stolen laptop — first, remote-lock it via Find My Mac, Windows Find My Device, or your antivirus tool. Change every password from a different device. Then file BOTH a campus police report (the kiosk wizard handles theft and property reports) and a renters / homeowners insurance claim. Save your serial number for both reports.

tiles.label: Stolen phone
tiles.subtitle: Remote-lock + cellular suspend
tiles.spokenText: For a stolen phone — remote-lock via Find My iPhone (iCloud) or Find My Device (Google). Call your carrier to suspend cellular service. File a police report (the kiosk wizard handles theft as well as safety incidents). If you used the phone for two-factor authentication, contact IT to switch your 2FA to backup codes before someone uses the device to break into your accounts.

tiles.label: Software access
tiles.subtitle: Microsoft 365 / Adobe
tiles.spokenText: For free or discounted software — most campuses include free Microsoft 365 (Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook) for enrolled students. Adobe Creative Cloud, MATLAB, SPSS, and other major tools are often available through the campus software portal. Sign in to the IT website with your campus ID to see what is available.

tiles.label: Printer credits
tiles.subtitle: Add money / paper jam
tiles.spokenText: For campus printing — most campuses give a small free quota of pages per semester. Beyond that, add money to your campus card. For paper jams or broken printers, IT or the campus library staff can clear most jams.

tiles.label: Loaner laptop
tiles.subtitle: My computer broke
tiles.spokenText: For a loaner laptop — if your computer broke or is being repaired, the campus library or IT help desk often loans laptops for the day, the week, or longer for documented hardship. Some institutions reserve loaner laptops for students with financial need. Ask the IT help desk.

tiles.label: Internet at home
tiles.subtitle: I can't get online off-campus
tiles.spokenText: If you need internet at home and cannot afford it, the federal Lifeline program reduces monthly phone or internet costs for eligible low-income households — apply at lifelinesupport.org. (Note: the Affordable Connectivity Program ended in 2024 and is no longer available.) Some campuses also loan mobile hotspot devices to students with documented financial need. Talk to the Dean of Students or financial aid.

tiles.label: Transcript, holds, enrollment, registration
tiles.spokenText: Transcript, holds, enrollment, registration

tiles.label: Transcript — official
tiles.subtitle: For another school / employer
tiles.spokenText: For an official transcript — request through the registrar website or Parchment / National Student Clearinghouse, which most campuses use. Official transcripts are sealed and sent directly to the receiving institution. There is usually a small fee. Allow 3 to 5 business days.

tiles.label: Transcript — unofficial
tiles.subtitle: For myself / advising
tiles.spokenText: For an unofficial transcript — log in to your student portal and download it for free. Unofficial transcripts are fine for advising, financial aid forms you fill out yourself, or your own records, but not accepted by other schools or most employers.

tiles.label: Account HOLD — cannot register
tiles.subtitle: Different kinds of holds
tiles.spokenText: Several different kinds of holds can block registration: financial holds (unpaid balance — bursar), immunization holds (missing records — health center), advising holds (need to meet advisor before registering — academic advising), library holds (overdue books or fines — library), or parking holds (unpaid citations — parking services). Check your student portal for the specific hold, then go to that office to clear it.

tiles.label: Immunization hold
tiles.subtitle: Records missing
tiles.spokenText: For an immunization hold — most campuses require MMR, meningitis, and sometimes COVID immunization records. Submit through the student health center portal. If you got vaccines at home, ask your home doctor or county health department for the records. Religious or medical exemptions are available at most institutions.

tiles.label: Financial hold
tiles.subtitle: Bursar / unpaid balance
tiles.spokenText: For a financial hold from the bursar — usually means there is an unpaid balance from a prior term. Pay it, set up a payment plan, or contact financial aid to see if there is aid available to cover it. Hold-lift timing varies by campus and payment method — ask the bursar how soon the hold will clear if you have a tight deadline (like registration closing).

tiles.label: Late registration
tiles.subtitle: After deadline
tiles.spokenText: For late registration — most campuses have a late-registration fee (usually fifty to a few hundred dollars) and a short window of weeks beyond the regular deadline. Beyond that, you may need permission from the Dean of Students. Late registration is usually possible — but the closer to the start of term, the more options close.

tiles.label: Wait-list a class
tiles.subtitle: It's full
tiles.spokenText: For wait-listing a full class — most registration systems have a wait-list option you can join. Order on the wait-list usually matters. Some professors will let extra students in on the first day; others stick to the cap.

tiles.label: Audit a class
tiles.subtitle: No grade / no credit
tiles.spokenText: For auditing a class — some campuses allow registered students to audit a course alongside their for-credit load. You attend but do not get a grade or credit, and the cost is sometimes lower. Submit through the registrar with the professor's approval.

tiles.label: Pass / fail option
tiles.subtitle: Pass = no GPA hit
tiles.spokenText: For taking a class pass / fail — also called credit / no-credit at some schools. The pass earns credit but does not affect your GPA. Useful for hard electives. There is usually a deadline (often a few weeks into the term) and a limit on how many classes you can pass-fail. Check with the registrar.

tiles.label: Enrollment verification
tiles.subtitle: For insurance / loans / visa
tiles.spokenText: For enrollment verification — proof that you are currently enrolled — most campuses generate this through the National Student Clearinghouse, accessed from your student portal. Free. Insurance companies and loan servicers usually accept it. For immigration / visa purposes, some agencies require a registrar letter or DSO letter instead of the generic Clearinghouse verification — check with the requesting agency first.

tiles.label: Office of the Registrar (One Stop)
tiles.subtitle: Wilbur Cross Building · 860-486-1111
tiles.spokenText: Office of the Registrar (One Stop). Address: Wilbur Cross Building, 233 Glenbrook Road, Unit 4077, Storrs, CT 06269. Phone: 860-486-1111.

tiles.label: Meal plan, allergies, complaints
tiles.spokenText: Meal plan, allergies, complaints

tiles.label: Change my meal plan
tiles.subtitle: Up / down / off
tiles.spokenText: For changing a meal plan — meal-plan change windows are usually early in the term and campus-specific, so check the dining services or student housing office right away. After the window closes, changes usually require a medical or financial reason. Submit through the dining services office or student housing office, depending on your campus.

tiles.label: Severe food allergy
tiles.subtitle: Disability + dining
tiles.spokenText: For a severe food allergy — celiac, nut, dairy, soy, etc. — register with both Disability Services AND Dining Services. Most campuses have dietitians who do one-on-one meal planning, and dedicated allergen-free stations or pre-prepared meals. With documentation, you can also request a modified meal plan or partial refund if dining cannot accommodate.

tiles.label: Religious dietary
tiles.subtitle: Halal · kosher · etc.
tiles.spokenText: For religious dietary needs — halal, kosher, Hindu vegetarian, Jain, etc. — Dining Services is the first-line stop. Most dining halls have at least one station or rotating menu that meets these needs. If Dining Services cannot accommodate your tradition after you ask, then escalate as a religious-accommodation request — through the chaplaincy office, the Office for Equity / DEI, or student affairs.

tiles.label: Vegetarian / vegan
tiles.subtitle: Standard options
tiles.spokenText: For vegetarian or vegan dining — most campuses have a vegetarian station and label vegan options. If the available options are insufficient for your needs, Dining Services can usually work with you to ensure there are enough nutritious vegan options at every meal.

tiles.label: Food poisoning report
tiles.subtitle: Document quickly
tiles.spokenText: For suspected food poisoning from a dining hall — first, see the student health center for treatment if you are sick. Then file a report with Dining Services. Most campuses take food-safety reports seriously. If multiple students get sick from the same meal, investigation may involve Dining, Environmental Health & Safety, Student Health, or the local health department, depending on the campus.

tiles.label: Dining complaint
tiles.subtitle: Quality / staff / cleanliness
tiles.spokenText: For a dining complaint — quality, staff conduct, cleanliness, food safety not amounting to illness — file through Dining Services, often via an online form or QR codes in the dining hall. Most institutions also have a student dining-advisory committee that meets monthly.

tiles.label: I cannot afford food
tiles.subtitle: Pantry + emergency
tiles.spokenText: I am food-insecure — I cannot afford food. The campus food pantry is usually free and confidential. The Dean of Students office may have emergency grants for food. CT 211 can help find off-campus food resources.

tiles.label: Career services tasks
tiles.spokenText: Career services tasks

tiles.label: Career counseling intake
tiles.subtitle: First-time visit
tiles.spokenText: For a first-time career counseling appointment — schedule through the Career Services portal or drop in during walk-in hours. Most campuses have career coaches who can help you explore majors, plan an internship search, or prepare for grad school. Free for current students.

tiles.label: Resume / CV review
tiles.subtitle: Free expert feedback
tiles.spokenText: For resume or CV review — Career Services usually offers free reviews by appointment, by drop-in, or through written-feedback tools. Many campuses also use Big Interview or VMock for asynchronous AI-assisted resume feedback. Bring a target job description if you have one.

tiles.label: Mock interview
tiles.subtitle: Practice with feedback
tiles.spokenText: For a mock interview — Career Services offers practice interviews with a coach who role-plays as the employer. Bring the actual job description if you have an upcoming interview. Many campuses also have InterviewStream or similar video-mock tools for asynchronous practice.

tiles.label: On-campus interview slot
tiles.subtitle: Employer visits
tiles.spokenText: For on-campus interview slots — when employers visit to interview students, slots usually open through Handshake or your campus career portal. Sign up early; slots fill fast. Some employers pre-screen — submit resume first, then they invite specific candidates.

tiles.label: Grad school application help
tiles.subtitle: Personal statement + recs
tiles.spokenText: For graduate school applications — Career Services and pre-graduate advising can help with: choosing programs, personal statement review, GRE / GMAT / LSAT / MCAT prep resources, letter-of-rec coordination, application timeline, fee waivers for low-income applicants. Start at least one term before deadlines.

tiles.label: Letter of recommendation
tiles.subtitle: Ask early + provide context
tiles.spokenText: For requesting a letter of recommendation — ask the professor or supervisor at least four to six weeks before the deadline. Provide them: a copy of your resume, the specific program or job you are applying to, what you want them to highlight, and a clear deadline. A polite reminder one week before the deadline is appropriate.

tiles.label: LinkedIn + networking
tiles.subtitle: Profile + outreach
tiles.spokenText: For LinkedIn and professional networking — Career Services often offers LinkedIn profile reviews and networking workshops. The campus alumni network is a strong source of informational interviews — most institutions have a portal connecting students to alumni willing to talk about their careers.

tiles.label: Internship search
tiles.subtitle: Paid / unpaid / credit
tiles.spokenText: For internship search — Handshake is the most common platform. Career Services can also flag specific employer relationships unique to your campus. For unpaid internships, check Fair Labor Standards Act guidelines: at most institutions and many states, unpaid private-sector internships have specific legal limits. Academic credit may be available.

tiles.label: Salary negotiation
tiles.subtitle: After offer received
tiles.spokenText: For salary negotiation — Career Services offers negotiation coaching, often through PayScale or AAUW Smart Start workshops. Research salary ranges on Levels.fyi, Glassdoor, BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook, or your campus career-outcomes data. Negotiation is normal and expected.

tiles.label: Career fair sign-up
tiles.subtitle: Prepare in advance
tiles.spokenText: For career fairs — sign up in advance through Handshake or your career portal. Review the employer list, prep a 30-second elevator pitch, bring printed resumes if employers might want them. Dress code is usually business or business-casual. Some fairs allow virtual attendance.

tiles.label: Public service careers
tiles.subtitle: AmeriCorps / Peace Corps / Teach for America
tiles.spokenText: For public-service and gap-year options — AmeriCorps and Peace Corps offer service positions for new graduates. Teach for America places teachers in high-need schools. Fellowships like Rhodes, Marshall, Truman, Fulbright, Watson are competitive but generously funded. The Office of National Fellowships or pre-grad advising helps with these applications.

tiles.label: Visa, work auth, travel, status
tiles.spokenText: Visa, work auth, travel, status

tiles.label: Travel signature on I-20 / DS-2019
tiles.subtitle: Before any international trip
tiles.spokenText: For a travel signature — your DSO must sign the third page of your I-20 (F-1) or your DS-2019 (J-1) before any international trip. The signature is valid for one year for current students, six months for those on OPT. Without it, you cannot re-enter the United States. ISSS usually requires a few business days; do not leave it until the last day.

tiles.label: International Student & Scholar Services (ISSS)
tiles.subtitle: 2019 Hillside Road · 860-486-3855
tiles.spokenText: International Student & Scholar Services (ISSS). Address: 2019 Hillside Road, Unit 1083, Storrs, CT 06269. Phone: 860-486-3855. Hours: M-F 8:30a-4:30p.

tiles.label: CPT — work in your field during studies
tiles.subtitle: Curricular Practical Training
tiles.spokenText: CPT — Curricular Practical Training — lets F-1 students work in their field of study during their program, when the work is an integral part of their curriculum (course credit or program requirement). It must be authorized by the DSO before you start work. Up to 12 months of full-time CPT before OPT eligibility is affected. Talk to ISSS early — usually one term before the work starts.

tiles.label: OPT — work after graduation
tiles.subtitle: Optional Practical Training
tiles.spokenText: OPT — Optional Practical Training — gives F-1 students up to 12 months of work authorization in their field, usually used after graduation. You can apply up to 90 days before your program end date. USCIS processing takes weeks to months. Plan ahead — without an approved EAD card, you cannot legally start work.

tiles.label: STEM OPT extension
tiles.subtitle: 24 extra months for STEM
tiles.spokenText: STEM OPT — gives an extra 24 months of work authorization on top of the standard 12-month OPT, if your degree is on the official STEM Designated Degree Program List AND your employer is enrolled in E-Verify. Apply at least 90 days before your current OPT expires. Specific paperwork required: a timely Form I-765 (Application for Employment Authorization) filed with USCIS, plus Form I-983 (Training Plan for STEM OPT Students) coordinated with your employer and your DSO.

tiles.label: H-1B cap-subject timing
tiles.subtitle: Annual lottery
tiles.spokenText: H-1B — the most common employer-sponsored work visa. Most employers must enter the H-1B lottery in early March of each year; selected applications can be filed starting April 1 for an October 1 start date. Plan ahead: discuss timing with your employer early, and if you are on OPT or STEM OPT, your bridge between expiration and H-1B start may need cap-gap protection. ISSS can advise.

tiles.label: Reduced course load (medical)
tiles.subtitle: Authorized below full-time
tiles.spokenText: For Reduced Course Load — RCL — authorization, if you need to drop below the full-time enrollment requirement for medical reasons, academic difficulty (initial difficulty with English language or US teaching methods, one term only), or completion of program in your final term, your DSO can authorize it in SEVIS. Without RCL authorization, dropping below full-time triggers status problems.

tiles.label: Re-entering the United States
tiles.subtitle: Documents to carry
tiles.spokenText: When re-entering the US from international travel, carry: passport (valid 6+ months), valid F-1 or J-1 visa stamp (unless on automatic visa revalidation), I-20 or DS-2019 with travel signature dated within the validity window, proof of enrollment (current transcript or registrar letter), and if on OPT or CPT, your EAD card and employment letter. Expect possible secondary inspection — answer questions honestly and ask for ISSS contact if confused.

tiles.label: Banking + SSN + driver license
tiles.subtitle: Setup once arrived
tiles.spokenText: Setting up life in the US — most banks accept international students with passport plus I-20 plus campus ID. For a Social Security Number, you need an on-campus job offer or CPT/OPT authorization — apply at the local SSA office. For a CT driver license, you need passport + I-20 + I-94 + proof of address. ISSS has detailed guides for each.

tiles.label: Tax filing for international students
tiles.subtitle: 1042-S + Form 8843
tiles.spokenText: For tax filing — even if you had no US income, F-1 and J-1 students must file Form 8843. If you earned US income, you also file 1040-NR. ISSS often offers free Sprintax software or arranges a free tax workshop. Tax year is January 1 - December 31; filing deadline is mid-April. Filing matters for future green-card applications.

tiles.label: SEVIS termination warning
tiles.subtitle: Time-sensitive — restoration
tiles.spokenText: If you have received a SEVIS termination warning, that is a time-sensitive emergency — the kiosk has a dedicated path for it.

tiles.label: Privacy + immigration enforcement
tiles.subtitle: FERPA + your rights
tiles.spokenText: Your enrollment records are protected by FERPA — schools generally may not release them without your consent unless a FERPA exception applies, including compliance with a lawfully issued subpoena or judicial order. An informal request from a federal agent, without a subpoena or court order, generally does not require disclosure. If ICE or USCIS comes to campus asking about you, you have the right to remain silent and the right to talk to a lawyer. Many CT institutions have policies committing to FERPA-compliance — ask in writing. Talk to ISSS or the campus civil rights office immediately if approached.

tiles.label: GI Bill, deployment, benefits
tiles.spokenText: GI Bill, deployment, benefits

tiles.label: Post-9/11 GI Bill
tiles.subtitle: Tuition + housing allowance
tiles.spokenText: The Post-9/11 GI Bill — Chapter 33 — pays tuition and fees directly to the school, plus a monthly housing allowance (MHA) based on the zip code of your school, plus a books and supplies stipend. Benefits are paid as long as you maintain enrollment. The campus veterans services office certifies your enrollment to the VA each term.

tiles.label: Yellow Ribbon program
tiles.subtitle: Tuition gap covered
tiles.spokenText: The Yellow Ribbon program closes the gap between Post-9/11 GI Bill cap and the actual tuition at private schools or out-of-state public schools. Both the school and the VA contribute to the gap. Some schools (including most CT public institutions) participate fully. Ask veterans services if your school participates and at what level.

tiles.label: Transfer GI Bill to spouse / child
tiles.subtitle: TEB — while still serving
tiles.spokenText: You can transfer your GI Bill benefits to a spouse or dependent child, but the request usually must be made while you are STILL serving. The standard requirement is 6 years served plus an additional 4-year service obligation, with limited exceptions (such as some Purple Heart cases). Once you separate without the request approved, you typically cannot start a new transfer. If you already transferred and need to manage the benefits, that is handled through milConnect.

tiles.label: Deployment-related withdrawal
tiles.subtitle: No academic penalty
tiles.spokenText: If you are called to active duty mid-semester, contact the registrar and veterans services as soon as you receive orders. Refund, leave of absence, readmission, and VA-benefit treatment depend on school policy and VA rules. Many CT institutions offer full tuition refund and protect academic standing for active-duty interruptions, but you should not assume — confirm in writing. USERRA is a federal employment-reemployment statute that may apply if you are also a campus employee.

tiles.label: Reserve / National Guard schedule conflict
tiles.subtitle: Drill weekends + class
tiles.spokenText: If your military drill or training conflicts with class schedule, USERRA and state law protect your reemployment after service. For shorter conflicts — like a single drill weekend or required training — talk to the professor early and provide documentation. Veterans services can help arrange make-up work.

tiles.label: ROTC contract question
tiles.subtitle: Scholarship + service obligation
tiles.spokenText: For Reserve Officers Training Corps — ROTC — questions about scholarship terms, service obligation, or contract changes, talk to your ROTC unit detachment AND veterans services. Some questions (like medical disqualification or branch change) involve both military and academic processes.

tiles.label: VA disability rating + accommodation
tiles.subtitle: Disability Services intersection
tiles.spokenText: If you have a VA disability rating — for PTSD, TBI, hearing loss, mobility issues, or others — it may support an academic-accommodation request through Disability Services. Most Disability Services offices also require current functional documentation from a qualified treating provider, not just the VA rating letter, to determine specific accommodations. Bring both. The Disability Services office is separate from veterans services but they coordinate. You do not have to disclose your military background to use accommodations.

tiles.label: Military service credit
tiles.subtitle: JST + ACE evaluation
tiles.spokenText: For military service credit — the American Council on Education (ACE) translates military training into college credit. Submit your Joint Services Transcript (JST) or Community College of the Air Force (CCAF) transcript to the registrar. Most schools accept ACE recommendations. Veterans services helps coordinate the evaluation.

tiles.label: PTSD / TBI mental health
tiles.subtitle: Vet Center + VA + CAPS
tiles.spokenText: For PTSD, TBI, or other mental-health support specifically for veterans — the Vet Center program operates community-based counseling at no cost (separate from VA Medical Centers). VA Mental Health is also available. Campus CAPS counselors often have veteran-specific training. Veterans Crisis Line: dial 988 and press 1.

tiles.label: Military spouse benefits
tiles.subtitle: MyCAA + EFMP
tiles.spokenText: Military spouse benefits — MyCAA covers up to $4,000 for portable career training for spouses of active duty E-1 to E-5, W-1 to W-2, and O-1 to O-2. EFMP (Exceptional Family Member Program) supports families with special needs. Spouse Career Advancement Account (SECO) provides career coaching. Veterans services on campus can refer.

tiles.label: SAP rules different for VA benefits
tiles.subtitle: Different appeal
tiles.spokenText: Reminder — Satisfactory Academic Progress rules for VA benefits are slightly different from federal Title IV financial aid SAP. The VA has its own SAP review and own appeal process through your school certifying official. If you have a SAP appeal involving GI Bill benefits, work with veterans services in addition to financial aid.

tiles.spokenText: Go back

tiles.label: Main
tiles.spokenText: Take me back to the main screen.

tiles.label: Holidays, prayer, dress, exams
tiles.spokenText: Holidays, prayer, dress, exams

tiles.label: Your right at federally-funded schools
tiles.subtitle: Title VI + institutional policy
tiles.spokenText: At federally-funded schools, Title VI of the Civil Rights Act (combined with Department of Education Office for Civil Rights guidance) addresses discrimination based on shared ancestry, ethnic characteristics, or national origin — which OCR has clarified can include religious-identity-based harassment. Most schools also have institutional policies that explicitly protect against religious discrimination and provide reasonable accommodations for religious observance. (If you are also a student employee, Title VII of the Civil Rights Act covers employment-based religious accommodations separately.) The specific process varies by school but the protections are broad.

tiles.label: Religious holiday — missing class
tiles.subtitle: Notify professor in advance
tiles.spokenText: For missing class due to religious observance — notify your professor in writing as early as possible in the term, ideally during the first two weeks. Most institutional policies require professors to provide a reasonable opportunity to make up missed work, including exams. Connecticut General Statute Section 10a-50 addresses this for public institutions.

tiles.label: Exam scheduled on holy day
tiles.subtitle: Request reschedule
tiles.spokenText: If a final exam or major assessment is scheduled on a religious holy day, you have the right to request a reschedule. Submit the request through the registrar or the Dean of Students. Provide the holiday name and date; you do not have to prove religious sincerity beyond the request itself.

tiles.label: Prayer space on campus
tiles.subtitle: Multifaith room
tiles.spokenText: Most campuses have multifaith prayer and meditation spaces. The chaplaincy office maintains the map. If yours does not exist or is inadequate (no ablution facilities for Muslim students, no wudu-compatible bathrooms, no quiet space for Jewish observance), this is a reasonable accommodation request through the chaplaincy + Office for Equity.

tiles.label: Fasting + academic scheduling
tiles.subtitle: Ramadan, Yom Kippur, Bahai
tiles.spokenText: If you are fasting for Ramadan, Yom Kippur, Bahai 19-day fast, or other religious observance, you can request: exam rescheduling so exams do not fall on the fast-breaking day or worst hour, dining hall extended hours for suhoor and iftar (Muslim students), or excused absence for the holiday itself. Notify professors and Dining Services in advance.

tiles.label: Religious dress
tiles.subtitle: Hijab, yarmulke, turban, etc.
tiles.spokenText: Religious dress — hijab, yarmulke, turban, kara, religious crosses, modest dress — is generally protected. If there is a conflict with a uniform (lab, ROTC, athletics), most institutions accommodate while maintaining safety. For accommodation, talk to the program / department lead first; escalate to Office for Equity / DEI if needed.

tiles.label: Religious dietary
tiles.subtitle: See Dining board
tiles.spokenText: For religious dietary needs at the dining hall — halal, kosher, Jain, etc. — Dining Services is the first stop. The kiosk has a dedicated dining board.

tiles.label: Sabbath / Saturday classes
tiles.subtitle: Sabbatarian accommodation
tiles.spokenText: If a course or required activity is scheduled on your Sabbath — Friday evening through Saturday evening for Jewish students, Saturday for Seventh-day Adventists and some other traditions — you can request an accommodation. The first step is the professor; if not resolved, the Office for Equity or chaplaincy escalates.

tiles.label: Office for Inclusion and Civil Rights (Title IX Coordinator)
tiles.subtitle: Wood Hall · 860-486-2943
tiles.spokenText: Office for Inclusion and Civil Rights (Title IX Coordinator). Address: Wood Hall, 241 Glenbrook Road, Unit 4175, Storrs, CT 06269. Phone: 860-486-2943. Hours: M-F 8a-5p.

tiles.label: Balancing work, family, school
tiles.spokenText: Balancing work, family, school

tiles.label: You are not alone
tiles.subtitle: Working / parenting / returning students
tiles.spokenText: You are not alone. About 1 in 5 Connecticut college students is 25 or older per recent CT Office of Higher Education enrollment data — and many more across all ages are working full-time, parenting, returning after years away, or balancing military service. The kiosk surfaces the resources that actually fit your life.

tiles.label: Evening + weekend programs
tiles.subtitle: Schedule around work
tiles.spokenText: For evening and weekend programs — many CT institutions have schedule formats designed for working students: evening classes, weekend cohorts, accelerated 8-week terms, hybrid (online + in-person). Talk to your advisor about which fits your schedule.

tiles.label: Credit for prior learning (CPL)
tiles.subtitle: Save time + money
tiles.spokenText: Credit for Prior Learning — also called PLA, portfolio assessment, or CLEP — lets you earn college credit for learning you have done outside of college: work experience, military service, certifications, life experience. Saves both time and money. The registrar handles the assessment. Ask early — assessment takes time.

tiles.label: Military service credit
tiles.subtitle: ACE evaluation
tiles.spokenText: For military service credit — the American Council on Education (ACE) translates military training into college credit. Submit your Joint Services Transcript (JST) or Community College of the Air Force (CCAF) transcript to the registrar. Most schools accept ACE recommendations. Veterans services can help coordinate.

tiles.label: Employer tuition reimbursement
tiles.subtitle: Timing + payment
tiles.spokenText: For employer tuition reimbursement — many employers reimburse after you complete the course (not before). Some campuses offer "deferred billing" so you do not pay upfront and wait — they bill you AFTER your employer reimburses. Talk to the bursar about deferred-billing options.

tiles.label: Childcare options
tiles.subtitle: On + off campus
tiles.spokenText: For childcare while you study — some campuses have on-site child-care centers with student priority and sliding-scale fees. Off-campus options often have CT-subsidized rates through CT Care 4 Kids program. The Dean of Students office or Adult / Non-Traditional Student program coordinator can help connect you.

tiles.label: Adult / non-trad student center
tiles.subtitle: Community + advising
tiles.spokenText: Some campuses have a dedicated Adult / Non-Traditional Student program — community space, dedicated advising, evening hours, peer mentoring. Worth asking about even if not heavily advertised. The Dean of Students office knows what is available.

tiles.label: Lactation / parenting space
tiles.subtitle: Title IX-protected
tiles.spokenText: For parenting students — Title IX protections cover pregnancy, childbirth, and lactation. The pregnant-student board has the full path.

tiles.spokenText: Dean of Students Office. Address: Wilbur Cross Building, Suite 102, 233 Glenbrook Road, Unit 4062, Storrs, CT 06269. Phone: 860-486-3426. Hours: 8a-5p.

tiles.label: Hidden curriculum + support
tiles.spokenText: Hidden curriculum + support

tiles.label: First-gen is a strength
tiles.subtitle: Not a deficit
tiles.spokenText: Being first-generation in college means your family has not done this before — so you are figuring out things that other students learn from parents. This is not a deficit. It is a skill: navigating new institutions without a map. The kiosk surfaces what nobody tells you.

tiles.label: The "hidden curriculum"
tiles.subtitle: What nobody says
tiles.spokenText: The hidden curriculum is the unwritten rules of college: how to email a professor, when to go to office hours (yes — always), how to ask for help, what a credit hour means, when to ask for an extension and how, what a TA actually does. None of it is in the catalog. Ask. Every other student is also confused.

tiles.label: How to email a professor
tiles.subtitle: Format + tone
tiles.spokenText: Emailing a professor — keep it short, professional, and clear. Subject line specific. Greeting: "Dear Professor LastName" or "Dr. LastName". Identify yourself: name, class, section. State the request. Sign off "Best, FirstName LastName, student ID." Expect a reply within a few business days; do not double-email before then.

tiles.label: Office hours — go!
tiles.subtitle: Not just for problems
tiles.spokenText: Office hours are dedicated time professors set aside to talk to students. Going is normal and expected. You do not need to have a specific question or problem — you can also go to discuss the field, ask about research, or just be known to the professor. Letters of rec come from professors who know you.

tiles.label: First-gen student programs
tiles.subtitle: Community + mentorship
tiles.spokenText: Most institutions have a first-generation student program — community space, peer mentorship, dedicated advising, social events. National First-Gen College Celebration is November 8 each year. Look for a TRIO Student Support Services office or McNair Scholars program — federal programs specifically for first-gen and low-income students.

tiles.label: Financial aid — you may qualify for more
tiles.subtitle: Beyond Pell
tiles.spokenText: Beyond the Pell Grant — many first-gen students miss out on additional aid: state grants (CT has the Roberta B. Willis Scholarship for low-income students), institutional grants tied to first-gen status, work-study, and outside scholarships specifically for first-gen students. Talk to financial aid about ALL the options.

tiles.label: Grad school — yes, it is for you
tiles.subtitle: McNair + PhD pipeline
tiles.spokenText: Graduate school is more accessible than you might think — especially PhD programs in academic fields, which pay you (no tuition + stipend). McNair Scholars program specifically prepares first-gen / low-income students for PhD applications. Talk to a faculty member you respect — they can connect you with research opportunities.

tiles.label: Imposter syndrome
tiles.subtitle: You belong here
tiles.spokenText: Imposter syndrome — feeling like you do not belong, that you got in by mistake, that everyone is smarter — is common in first-gen students. It is not the truth. You got in because you earned it. Most successful people have felt this. Talk to a CAPS counselor familiar with the experience.

tiles.label: Career — networking is taught
tiles.subtitle: Not assumed
tiles.spokenText: Networking and career navigation are SKILLS — not innate. Career Services teaches them. Resume, LinkedIn, informational interviews, salary negotiation — all of these are learnable. Use the resources.

tiles.label: Connecticut-specific resources
tiles.spokenText: Connecticut-specific resources

tiles.label: You have a path in CT
tiles.subtitle: In-state tuition + state aid
tiles.spokenText: Connecticut is one of about 24 states that extends in-state tuition to undocumented students who meet specific criteria — typically graduating from a CT high school after attending for a set number of years. Connecticut Public Act 11-43 (2011) created the in-state tuition path, with later acts (including PA 15-82) refining the criteria. Connecticut Public Act 18-2 opened institutional financial aid at public CT institutions for certain undocumented students, subject to state-law criteria. Eligibility depends on the specific statute — verify with admissions or financial aid. You are not alone; there is a community here.

tiles.label: WHO to disclose to
tiles.subtitle: Be careful
tiles.spokenText: Important: be careful who knows your status. Confidential resources — campus counselors in their treatment role, designated victim advocates, attorneys — generally must keep what you share private (subject to standard legal/safety exceptions). Mandatory reporters do NOT keep disclosures private. Many CT institutions treat undocumented-student-program coordinators and specifically-trained financial aid officers as confidential or limited-disclosure for this purpose — but it varies by school. Confirm with them directly before disclosing: ask "Is what I tell you confidential, and if so, what exceptions apply?" Random staff members or peers usually are not bound by confidentiality.

tiles.label: FERPA + immigration
tiles.subtitle: School records are protected
tiles.spokenText: Your enrollment records at the school are protected by FERPA — Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act. Schools generally may not disclose FERPA-protected records without consent unless a FERPA exception applies, including compliance with a lawfully issued subpoena or judicial order. An informal request from a federal agent without a subpoena or court order generally does not require disclosure. Many CT institutions have policies that clarify their FERPA-compliance practices — ask the registrar for the policy in writing.

tiles.label: In-state tuition in CT
tiles.subtitle: PA 11-43 / PA 18-2
tiles.spokenText: Connecticut Public Act 11-43 (2011), with later amendments including PA 15-82, generally extends in-state tuition rates to undocumented students who meet specific criteria — typically attending a CT high school for a set number of years, graduating from a CT high school, and signing an affidavit. The exact criteria depend on the current statute; verify with admissions before assuming eligibility. Apply through admissions or the registrar; do not be afraid to ask. The savings can be tens of thousands of dollars.

tiles.label: CT state institutional aid
tiles.subtitle: PA 18-2
tiles.spokenText: Connecticut Public Act 18-2 (2018) opened access to state institutional aid at public CT institutions for certain undocumented students, subject to state-law criteria. You generally cannot receive federal financial aid (no FAFSA), but state institutional aid AND outside scholarships fill significant gaps. Talk to a financial aid officer who has been trained in undocumented-student support.

tiles.label: DACA renewal
tiles.subtitle: Every 2 years
tiles.spokenText: DACA — Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals — must be renewed every two years. Start the renewal process 150 days before expiration. The fee changes; CHIRLA and other immigration legal nonprofits offer free help with renewals. USCIS continues to accept both initial and renewal DACA filings, but as of mid-2026 currently only approves renewals — initial applications are accepted but held pending. Talk to an immigration attorney before filing initial.

tiles.label: TheDream.US scholarship
tiles.subtitle: For DACA + TPS students
tiles.spokenText: TheDream.US is the largest scholarship program for DACA and TPS students. Current National Scholarship awards are up to about $16,500 for an associate degree or $33,000 for a bachelor degree at participating National Partner Colleges. Verify current award amounts at thedream.us. Many CT institutions are partners.

tiles.label: Other scholarships — no status required
tiles.subtitle: HSF, MALDEF, etc.
tiles.spokenText: Many scholarships do not require immigration status verification — Hispanic Scholarship Fund, MALDEF, Golden Door Scholars, Educators for Fair Consideration. The campus financial aid office and the undocumented-student program coordinator can connect you with the full list.

tiles.label: Free legal help
tiles.subtitle: CIRA + IRIS + clinics
tiles.spokenText: Free immigration legal help in CT — Connecticut Immigrant Rights Alliance (CIRA), Integrated Refugee and Immigrant Services (IRIS) in New Haven, Yale Law School and UConn Law School immigration clinics. The Connecticut Bar Association has a referral service. For urgent matters, AILA (American Immigration Lawyers Association) has a directory.

tiles.label: If ICE comes to campus
tiles.subtitle: Your rights
tiles.spokenText: If ICE or a federal agent approaches you or comes to campus: you have the right to remain silent. You can say "I am exercising my right to remain silent." You can ask "Am I free to leave?" — if yes, walk away calmly. Do not sign anything before legal review. Ask to speak with a lawyer (note: in immigration proceedings, attorney representation is at no cost to the government — you must pay your own or work with free legal nonprofits). Do not lie or run. Some CT campuses publish welcoming-campus or privacy policies, but legal "sanctuary" status varies — do not assume your campus has formal legal protection. Contact the Dean of Students or an immigration attorney immediately. Save the legal-help phone numbers from this kiosk in your phone NOW.

tiles.label: Dean of Students Office
tiles.subtitle: Wilbur Cross Building · 860-486-3426
tiles.spokenText: Dean of Students Office. Address: Wilbur Cross Building, Suite 102, 233 Glenbrook Road, Unit 4062, Storrs, CT 06269. Phone: 860-486-3426. Hours: 8a-5p.

tiles.label: United We Dream hotline
tiles.spokenText: United We Dream MigraWatch hotline — 1-844-363-1423 — connects with rapid-response support for ICE encounters. Save this number.

tiles.label: Mental health (confidential)
tiles.subtitle: CAPS does not report status
tiles.spokenText: Campus counseling — CAPS — is generally confidential in their treatment role, subject to standard legal and safety exceptions (such as imminent danger or mandated reporting of child or elder abuse). Counselors are not immigration officers and the purpose of treatment is your wellbeing, not status verification. Many counselors are specifically trained in undocumented-student mental-health.

tiles.label: CT Safe Connect / CCADV — 24/7
tiles.subtitle: Call or text 1-888-774-2900
tiles.spokenText: CT Safe Connect is the statewide hotline run by the Connecticut Coalition Against Domestic Violence. Call or text 1-888-774-2900. Free, confidential, twenty-four hours, in English. For Spanish, 1-844-831-9200. They connect you to all eighteen CCADV member shelter programs and help with bed-finding, safety planning, transportation, and crisis counseling. If you are leaving an abusive partner, family member, or housemate, this is the right first call. Deaf or hard-of-hearing callers can use 7-1-1 relay or VRS.

tiles.label: Interval House — 24/7
tiles.spokenText: Interval House — one of the largest DV shelters in CT, serving Greater Hartford. Twenty-four hour hotline 860-838-8467. They also have community-based services if you do not need shelter.

tiles.label: SANE exam tonight
tiles.subtitle: Sexual assault forensic nurse
tiles.spokenText: For a Sexual Assault Nurse Examiner exam tonight: call the Connecticut Alliance to End Sexual Violence — formerly CONNSACS — at 1-888-999-5545 in English or 1-888-568-8332 in Spanish. They will route you to the nearest CT SANE-program hospital and send an advocate to be with you. The exam is free, regardless of whether you choose to report to police. To preserve evidence: do not shower, do not change clothes, do not douche, and if possible avoid using the bathroom before the exam.

tiles.label: National DV Hotline — 24/7
tiles.subtitle: 1-800-799-7233 · text START to 88788
tiles.spokenText: National Domestic Violence Hotline. 1-800-799-7233. For Deaf callers, video-phone 1-855-812-1001 or use 7-1-1 relay. Text START to 88788. Free, confidential, twenty-four hours. Useful if you are relocating out of Connecticut or want a second option alongside the CT statewide line.

tiles.label: Human Trafficking — 24/7
tiles.subtitle: 1-888-373-7888 · text HELP to 233733
tiles.spokenText: National Human Trafficking Hotline. 1-888-373-7888 or text HELP to 233733. They can connect trafficking survivors with anti-trafficking advocates in Connecticut who help plan a safer exit and look for safe housing options. Twenty-four hours, confidential.

tiles.label: No shelter bed tonight?
tiles.subtitle: Ask hotline about options
tiles.spokenText: If shelter beds are full in your area, the CT Safe Connect hotline can help look for other options — including possible emergency hotel placement through partner agencies. Availability is never guaranteed, but ask directly: "are there any other safe-housing options for tonight?"

tiles.label: Safety planning conversation
tiles.subtitle: 24/7 hotline staff trained
tiles.spokenText: A safety plan is a personalized step-by-step for getting yourself (and children, pets) out safely. CCADV and NDVH hotline staff are trained to walk you through one — what to pack, where to go first, what to leave behind, what to tell whom. This is free and takes thirty to sixty minutes.

tiles.label: Stay with someone you trust
tiles.subtitle: CCADV can advise on safety
tiles.spokenText: If you have a friend or family member you trust to stay with, that is a valid option — but tell the CCADV hotline so they can help with the safety plan. The abuser may know about that person; CCADV will help you think it through.

tiles.label: CT survivor-protection paths
tiles.subtitle: 3 court orders + 1 address program
tiles.spokenText: Connecticut law gives survivors several distinct protections. There are three different court orders — a Civil Restraining Order, a Civil Protection Order, and a Criminal Protective Order — plus the Address Confidentiality Program, which is not a court order but hides your address on public records. Each one is for a different situation. The kiosk will help you find the right path.

tiles.label: Civil restraining order
tiles.subtitle: Family Court — family + household
tiles.spokenText: A Civil Restraining Order — Form JD-FM-137 — is filed in Family Court, the Superior Court Family Division. Eligibility: the person you fear is a family or household member — spouse, ex-spouse, parent, child, sibling, current or former dating partner, or housemate. Free to file. The court may grant an Ex Parte temporary order the same day; a full hearing follows within fourteen days.

tiles.label: Civil protection order
tiles.subtitle: Superior Court — stalking + sexual assault
tiles.spokenText: A Civil Protection Order is for stalking, sexual assault, or repeated patterns of harassment where the person you fear is NOT a family or household member — for example, a coworker, classmate, neighbor, or stranger. Filed in Superior Court, civil division. Free. The court evaluates the application; a hearing follows. Connecticut Legal Services and the Judicial Branch self-help center can walk you through the paperwork.

tiles.label: Criminal protective order
tiles.subtitle: May be issued in a criminal case
tiles.spokenText: When criminal charges are filed against the person who harmed you — for example, after an arrest for assault, threatening, or stalking — a judge may issue a Criminal Protective Order as part of that case. The prosecutor handles it; you do not file it yourself. Conditions can include no contact and stay-away orders. Talk to the Office of the Victim Advocate or your case prosecutor about your rights and how to be heard.

tiles.label: Address Confidentiality Program (ACP)
tiles.subtitle: Hide your address — not a court order
tiles.spokenText: The Connecticut Address Confidentiality Program — ACP — gives survivors a substitute mailing address to use on public records, so the abuser cannot find them through DMV, voter rolls, court filings, or other records. ACP is not a court order; it is a separate program administered by the CT Secretary of the State. Application requires working with an enrolling agency — most CCADV member shelters are enrolling agencies. Call 1-888-774-2900 for help getting started.

tiles.label: Other safety tools — by situation
tiles.subtitle: Guns · stalking · online · property
tiles.spokenText: If your situation does not match the three court orders or ACP cleanly: if guns are present in the home, ask police about a Connecticut Risk Protection Order — sometimes called a risk warrant — which is officer or family-initiated. If this is stalking or assault by someone who is not an intimate partner, ask legal aid about the Civil Protection Order path. If the contact is online — texts, social media, or platforms — save screenshots first and ask legal aid what to document. CT Legal Services at 1-800-453-3320 can help you figure out the right path for your facts.

tiles.label: OVS — Victim Compensation
tiles.subtitle: State pays for crime costs
tiles.spokenText: Connecticut Office of Victim Services — OVS — provides financial compensation for crime victims for medical bills, counseling, lost wages, funeral costs, relocation expenses, and more. Apply within two years of the crime (longer for some categories). Application is free. Search "CT Office of Victim Services" or call the OVS hotline.

tiles.label: VAWA self-petition
tiles.subtitle: Battered immigrant spouse / child / parent
tiles.spokenText: The Violence Against Women Act — VAWA — allows certain abused immigrant spouses, children, and parents of US citizens or lawful permanent residents to self-petition for status, independent of the abusive family member. Eligibility is not limited by gender — cisgender men and trans people may also qualify. Connecticut immigration legal services such as IRIS in New Haven, CIRI (the Connecticut Institute for Refugees and Immigrants) in Bridgeport, and the Yale and UConn law school immigration clinics can help with VAWA petitions at no cost.

tiles.label: U-visa for crime victims
tiles.subtitle: Crime victim immigration relief
tiles.spokenText: The U-visa provides temporary lawful status for certain crime victims — including domestic violence, sexual assault, and trafficking victims — who help law enforcement. You will need a law enforcement certification, usually signed by the investigating detective or prosecutor. CT-based free immigration legal services such as IRIS, CIRI, and the Yale and UConn law school immigration clinics can help with U-visa petitions.

tiles.label: CT Legal Services
tiles.subtitle: Free civil legal help
tiles.spokenText: Connecticut Legal Services and Statewide Legal Services. Free legal help for low-income survivors on housing, family law, public benefits. 1-800-453-3320.

tiles.label: CT VINE — release notification
tiles.subtitle: Register at vinelink.com
tiles.spokenText: CT VINE — Victim Information and Notification Everyday — sends an automated alert when the person in custody is released, transferred, or has a court hearing. Register online at vinelink.com (look for Connecticut), or ask the CT Department of Correction Victim Services Office for the current registration phone number. Free and confidential.

tiles.label: Material help — food, money, utilities
tiles.spokenText: Material help — food, money, utilities

tiles.label: I need 911 NOW
tiles.subtitle: Press at any time
tiles.spokenText: I need 911 right now. Please call 911 immediately.

tiles.label: CT 211 — call right now
tiles.subtitle: Statewide info + referral
tiles.spokenText: Dial 2-1-1 in Connecticut. Free, twenty-four hours. CT 211 is the central referral hub — food, housing, utility help, child care, transportation, mental-health services. They know what is available in your specific town this week.

tiles.label: Food pantry — local
tiles.subtitle: 211 routes
tiles.spokenText: For local food pantries, dial 211 and press 1 for food. They will route you to the nearest pantry by your town. Most pantries are open weekly and free — no income proof needed at most.

tiles.label: OVS emergency funds
tiles.subtitle: CT Office of Victim Services
tiles.spokenText: CT Office of Victim Services has emergency funds for crime victims for immediate needs — relocation, security deposit, medical co-pays, mental-health services. Apply through OVS directly or through a CCADV member shelter / sexual-assault crisis center, which can submit on your behalf.

tiles.label: SNAP (food stamps)
tiles.subtitle: Apply online
tiles.spokenText: SNAP — Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program — covers groceries. Apply through CT Department of Social Services at ct.gov/dss or at any DSS office. If you are fleeing abuse, you can apply even if you are still legally part of the abuser household — talk to a DSS worker about emergency expedited processing.

tiles.label: TFA / cash assistance
tiles.subtitle: Temporary Family Assistance
tiles.spokenText: Temporary Family Assistance — TFA — provides monthly cash assistance for low-income families with children. Apply through CT DSS. Survivors fleeing abuse can often get expedited processing.

tiles.label: SSDI — disability income
tiles.subtitle: Work-history based
tiles.spokenText: Social Security Disability Insurance — SSDI — is monthly federal income for people who can no longer work due to a long-term medical condition AND have enough recent work history. Apply at ssa.gov or any CT Social Security office. Survivors with PTSD, traumatic brain injury, severe depression, anxiety, or physical injuries from abuse may qualify. Many people are denied the first time and need to appeal — CT Legal Services or a NOSSCR-affiliated disability representative may be able to help, often for free or on contingency.

tiles.label: SSI — needs-based income
tiles.subtitle: No work history needed
tiles.spokenText: Supplemental Security Income — SSI — is monthly federal income for people with a disability OR age 65+, with very low income AND very few assets. No work history required. Children with disabilities may also qualify. Apply through SSA at ssa.gov or any CT office. Children who get SSI may also qualify for HUSKY, but in Connecticut you may need a separate Medicaid or HUSKY application through DSS or Access Health CT. CT Legal Services helps with applications and appeals.

tiles.label: Medicare — health coverage
tiles.subtitle: Age 65 or 24-mo SSDI entitlement
tiles.spokenText: Medicare is federal health coverage. Most people qualify at age 65. If you are entitled to SSDI, Medicare usually starts after 24 months of SSDI benefit entitlement, which is not always 24 months after your approval date — retroactive approvals can change the clock. Earlier eligibility for end-stage renal disease or ALS. Four parts: A hospital, B doctor, C Advantage plans, D drugs. The Center for Medicare Advocacy in Connecticut helps with denials. CHOICES — Connecticut’s SHIP program — through Aging and Disability Services and the Area Agencies on Aging, gives free, unbiased Medicare help to people with Medicare and their families or caregivers.

tiles.label: Utility shut-off help
tiles.subtitle: CEAP + winter protection
tiles.spokenText: Connecticut Energy Assistance Program — CEAP — helps low-income households with heating costs. Connecticut also has a winter shut-off protection that prevents utility disconnection November to May for eligible households. 211 routes you to the application path.

tiles.label: Clothing + basic supplies
tiles.subtitle: DV shelters often have
tiles.spokenText: For clothing, hygiene supplies, baby supplies, school supplies — most CCADV member shelters maintain donation rooms even if you are not staying overnight. Some Goodwill / Salvation Army / community closets also have free vouchers for survivors. 211 has the local listing.

tiles.label: Locksmith / security cost
tiles.subtitle: OVS may cover
tiles.spokenText: If you need to change locks, add security cameras, or otherwise make your home safer because the abuser had access, OVS emergency funds can sometimes cover these costs. Save receipts and apply.

tiles.label: Main
tiles.spokenText: Take me back to the main screen.

tiles.label: Children, school, custody, DCF
tiles.spokenText: Children, school, custody, DCF

tiles.label: I need 911 NOW
tiles.subtitle: Press at any time
tiles.spokenText: I need 911 right now. Please call 911 immediately.

tiles.label: Child in immediate danger
tiles.subtitle: 911 FIRST · then DCF Careline
tiles.spokenText: If a child is in immediate physical danger, call 911 first. To report ongoing child abuse or neglect to the state, also call the Connecticut DCF Careline at 1-800-842-2288, twenty-four hours. DCF accepts reports from anyone, not only mandated reporters.

tiles.label: Bringing kids to shelter
tiles.subtitle: CCADV shelters take children
tiles.spokenText: Most CCADV member DV shelters accept children — bedrooms accommodate parent-plus-children, and many have on-site childcare during the day. Call 1-888-774-2900 to confirm bed availability for you AND your kids.

tiles.label: Tell school about safety changes
tiles.subtitle: Pickup + custody updates
tiles.spokenText: Notify your child's school of the situation — who is authorized to pick up your child, any custody changes, the school's response if the abuser comes to the building. Many CT schools have established DV / custody protocols. Bring any court orders.

tiles.label: Emergency custody / parenting orders
tiles.subtitle: Family Court — same day
tiles.spokenText: For emergency custody or emergency parenting plan changes, you can file an Ex Parte motion in Family Court the same day. Family Court counselors (often called Family Relations) help walk you through the forms. CT Legal Services at 1-800-453-3320 can also help low-income survivors.

tiles.label: Childcare while you stabilize
tiles.subtitle: CT Care 4 Kids
tiles.spokenText: Connecticut Care 4 Kids subsidizes childcare for low-income working parents, parents in job training, and parents fleeing DV. Apply at ct.gov/oec. Some shelters have on-site childcare; CT Care 4 Kids can sometimes start immediately for DV survivors.

tiles.label: Therapy for children
tiles.subtitle: Trauma-informed for kids
tiles.spokenText: For child mental-health support after witnessing or experiencing abuse: CCADV member shelters often have child therapists on staff or partnerships with trauma-informed providers. CT 211 also lists child-trauma therapists by region. Some specifically use evidence-based modalities like Trauma-Focused CBT.

tiles.label: Kept from my children
tiles.subtitle: Other parent will not return them
tiles.spokenText: If the other parent is keeping you from your children in a way that goes against a custody order or court agreement, do not try to handle it alone. Document everything — dates, times, what was said, who saw it. Contact your family law attorney, or if you do not have one, CT Legal Services at 1-800-453-3320. If the situation is acute and you believe your child is at risk, call 911.

tiles.label: Birth certificates + IDs
tiles.subtitle: For new school enrollment
tiles.spokenText: If you fled without your children's birth certificates or IDs, you can enroll children in CT public school WITHOUT them — under McKinney-Vento (federal homeless law) and CT-specific protections, schools must enroll children of families in transition. Tell the school registrar "we are in transition."

tiles.label: Body + mind — short term and long
tiles.spokenText: Body + mind — short term and long

tiles.label: I need 911 NOW
tiles.subtitle: Press at any time
tiles.spokenText: I need 911 right now. Please call 911 immediately.

tiles.label: SANE exam — find nearest
tiles.subtitle: Sexual assault forensic care
tiles.spokenText: SANE — Sexual Assault Nurse Examiner — is a specialized forensic exam, free, regardless of whether you choose to report to police. To find the SANE-program hospital nearest you and get advocate support during the exam, call the Connecticut Alliance to End Sexual Violence at 1-888-999-5545 in English or 1-888-568-8332 in Spanish. Yale-New Haven Hospital operates a SANE program; many other CT hospitals do as well — the Alliance hotline knows which sites are currently active. To preserve evidence: do not shower, do not change clothes, do not douche, and if possible avoid using the bathroom before the exam.

tiles.label: Strangled / choked — go to ER
tiles.subtitle: Even if you feel okay now
tiles.spokenText: If someone put pressure on your neck — or you had trouble breathing, speaking, or swallowing, you passed out, or your vision went dark — please go to an emergency room now, even if you feel okay. Strangulation can cause delayed internal injuries that do not show right away: airway swelling, voice changes, swallowing problems, breathing difficulties, brain injury, and stroke risk. Many emergency rooms and SANE programs have specific strangulation evaluation protocols — ask for one.

tiles.label: Urgent / emergency care
tiles.subtitle: ER vs urgent care
tiles.spokenText: For acute injuries — go to the emergency room. For less acute injuries that still need same-day care — urgent care clinics. CT also has Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHCs) like Charter Oak Health Center that provide free or sliding-scale care regardless of insurance status.

tiles.label: Plan B — within 72 hours
tiles.subtitle: Over the counter · any pharmacy
tiles.spokenText: Plan B is an emergency-contraception pill, sold over the counter without a prescription at any pharmacy. It is most effective within seventy-two hours after unprotected sex, including sexual assault. SANE exams often offer it during the visit. Planned Parenthood at 1-800-230-7526 also provides it free or on a sliding scale.

tiles.label: ella — within 120 hours
tiles.subtitle: Prescription only — longer window
tiles.spokenText: ella is a different emergency-contraception medication that is effective up to one hundred twenty hours — five days — after unprotected sex. It requires a prescription. A clinician at the SANE program, Planned Parenthood at 1-800-230-7526, or an urgent care clinic can prescribe it. Some pharmacies stock it; others may need to order it.

tiles.label: STI testing + PEP
tiles.subtitle: PEP within 72 hours
tiles.spokenText: After sexual assault, STI testing and post-exposure prophylaxis — PEP for HIV — should happen within seventy-two hours for PEP effectiveness. SANE programs handle this. Without a SANE exam, urgent care or Planned Parenthood can also provide PEP and STI testing.

tiles.label: DV-aware counseling
tiles.subtitle: Free at CCADV shelters
tiles.spokenText: CCADV member shelters all provide free counseling for survivors — both individual therapy and support groups. The counselors are trauma-informed and DV-specialized. You do not need to be staying at a shelter to use the counseling. Call 1-888-774-2900.

tiles.label: Sexual assault counseling
tiles.subtitle: CT Alliance member centers
tiles.spokenText: For sexual-assault-specialized counseling: the member centers of the Connecticut Alliance to End Sexual Violence — formerly CONNSACS — provide free counseling across the state. Call 1-888-999-5545 in English or 1-888-568-8332 in Spanish for the nearest center.

tiles.label: 988 — crisis right now
tiles.subtitle: Suicide + crisis lifeline
tiles.spokenText: If you are in mental-health crisis right now — overwhelmed, suicidal thoughts, panic attacks — call or text 988. Free, confidential, twenty-four hours. The counselors are trained to support crime and DV survivors.

tiles.label: OVS pays for therapy
tiles.subtitle: Reimbursed by state
tiles.spokenText: CT Office of Victim Services compensation can pay for mental-health therapy related to the crime — including with off-campus therapists you choose. Save receipts. Apply through OVS.

tiles.label: Pregnancy options
tiles.subtitle: All-options counseling
tiles.spokenText: If you are or might be pregnant: All-Options at 1-888-493-0092 provides free, judgment-free pregnancy options counseling without pushing any specific direction. Planned Parenthood at 1-800-230-7526 also handles full options. Connecticut’s shield law — Public Act 22-19 — protects providers and people who help Connecticut residents access reproductive health care.
