tiles.label: Housing, work, immigration, financial security
tiles.spokenText: Housing, work, immigration, financial security

tiles.label: I need 911 NOW
tiles.subtitle: Press at any time
tiles.spokenText: I need 911 right now. Please call 911 immediately.

tiles.label: Transitional housing
tiles.subtitle: After shelter — before permanent
tiles.spokenText: Many CCADV member shelters operate transitional housing programs — typically up to two years — that bridge the gap between emergency shelter and permanent housing. Subsidized rent, support services, case management. Apply through your shelter or call CCADV 1-888-774-2900.

tiles.label: Permanent housing — CHFA
tiles.subtitle: CT Housing Finance Authority
tiles.spokenText: For longer-term housing assistance: CT Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) operates rental-assistance programs and first-time-homebuyer programs. The DV survivor program is specifically funded. Some CCADV shelters provide housing vouchers as part of transitional services.

tiles.label: CT Address Confidentiality Program
tiles.subtitle: ACP — for high-risk survivors
tiles.spokenText: The CT Address Confidentiality Program — ACP — gives you a substitute address for public records (DMV, voter rolls, court filings, school records). Useful when you need a permanent address but cannot let the abuser know it. Apply through an enrolling agency — most CCADV shelters are agencies. CT Secretary of the State administers.

tiles.label: Job training + employment
tiles.subtitle: CT Department of Labor
tiles.spokenText: CT Department of Labor and the American Job Center network offer free job training, resume help, and interview prep. CCADV member shelters also have employment specialists. Many DV survivors qualify for waivers of work requirements while stabilizing. CT 211 routes.

tiles.label: Credit + financial recovery
tiles.subtitle: Allstate Foundation + CFA
tiles.spokenText: Financial abuse is part of most DV — many survivors have damaged credit, joint debt with the abuser, or were prevented from working. The Allstate Foundation Moving Ahead curriculum (free, online) teaches financial recovery. CFA — Center for Financial Action — also has free financial counseling specifically for DV survivors.

tiles.label: Immigration — VAWA / U-visa / T-visa
tiles.subtitle: Free CT legal help
tiles.spokenText: For immigration relief paths — VAWA self-petition, U-visa, T-visa for trafficking survivors, SIJS for unaccompanied minors, asylum — free legal help in Connecticut is available through IRIS in New Haven, CIRI (the Connecticut Institute for Refugees and Immigrants) in Bridgeport, and the Yale and UConn law school immigration clinics. Apply early; these can take many months to several years.

tiles.label: Name change — legal
tiles.subtitle: Court process + ACP
tiles.spokenText: In extreme cases, survivors change their legal name to add another layer of separation from the abuser. CT Probate Court handles name changes. Combined with the Address Confidentiality Program, this can be effective. Cost: filing fee (waiver available for low income). Free legal help: CT Legal Services 1-800-453-3320.

tiles.label: Long-term advocate / case manager
tiles.subtitle: Ongoing support
tiles.spokenText: Most CCADV member shelters provide ongoing case management for months or years after the immediate crisis — court accompaniment, housing search, benefits applications, parenting support. Free. Call 1-888-774-2900 and ask about case-management services.

tiles.label: Survivors groups — peer support
tiles.subtitle: You are not alone
tiles.spokenText: Peer support groups — facilitated by other survivors who have been where you are — help with the long-term emotional recovery. CCADV member shelters run them; National DV Hotline can also connect you with online groups.

tiles.showForStaffText:
I AM DEAF AND USE AMERICAN SIGN LANGUAGE. PLEASE HELP ME CONNECT VIA VIDEO RELAY SERVICE (VRS) — IT IS FREE.

1) Call SORENSON VRS at 1-866-327-8877 from your phone.

3) The interpreter signs to me and speaks your words to you.

If you have a tablet, the SORENSON or CONVO RELAY app gives the same result faster. ZVRS, Convo, and GlobalVRS are all valid alternatives.

tiles.label: Before you drop
tiles.subtitle: Check 4 things
tiles.spokenText: Before you drop a class, please check four things: ONE — the registrar deadline. Drop after the deadline may show as a W on your transcript or you may still owe full tuition. TWO — financial aid impact. Dropping below half-time enrollment can affect future aid eligibility and may start federal loan grace periods (the six-month clock before you have to start repaying). Talk to financial aid BEFORE you drop. NOTE: complete withdrawal — dropping ALL your classes — is different. It can trigger a Return of Title IV Funds calculation where the school has to give back some federal aid the government already paid them. That is the case where you might end up owing money. A partial drop usually does not. THREE — academic standing: dropping below the required credit load may affect your standing, athletic eligibility, or visa status. FOUR — advisor sign-off: many programs require your advisor to approve the drop before the registrar will process it.

You have rights through this process — to bring an advisor, to receive supportive measures even if you do not want an investigation, and to choose informal resolution before a full hearing. The Title IX coordinator will explain each step. You can also pause or withdraw your report — but evidence the school gathers may stay in the record.

tiles.label: Perpetrator is faculty / coach / staff
tiles.spokenText: Perpetrator is faculty / coach / staff

tiles.label: You have additional rights
tiles.subtitle: Employment law + Title IX
tiles.spokenText: When the person who harmed you is a faculty member, coach, or staff member, the school has TWO legal obligations — Title IX and employment law. That can give you more options for protection but it can also make the process more complex. Many institutions involve Human Resources, the Provost's office, and the relevant Dean alongside the Title IX coordinator.

tiles.label: They give me grades / control my funding
tiles.subtitle: Urgent academic protection
tiles.spokenText: The person who harmed me is in my grade-giving chain, or they control my teaching assistantship, research grant, or dissertation. I need supportive measures right away — academic protection cannot wait. The Title IX office can put these in place WITHOUT you filing a formal complaint: section change, alternate exam proctor, no-contact order, payroll moved out of their chain.

tiles.label: Human Resources
tiles.subtitle: Employee discipline path
tiles.spokenText: Human Resources handles the employment side of the complaint. Title IX and HR usually coordinate; you can ask both to be involved. HR has separate procedures for faculty (often through the Provost) versus staff. Ask the Title IX office to connect you, or contact HR directly through the campus directory.

tiles.label: Provost / Dean's office
tiles.subtitle: Faculty discipline chain
tiles.spokenText: If the person who harmed you is a faculty member, the Provost's office or the Dean of the school they teach in usually has authority over their employment. This is separate from the Title IX investigation but often runs alongside it.

tiles.label: Conflict-of-interest concern
tiles.subtitle: Same office adjudicates both?
tiles.spokenText: If the Title IX office that would investigate is itself in the same chain as the person who harmed you — for example, if they report to the same Dean — you can ask for an outside investigator or for the case to be referred to a peer institution. You also have the right to a Title IX coordinator-designee who is not the regular coordinator.

tiles.label: Faculty union note
tiles.subtitle: AAUP / due process
tiles.spokenText: If the faculty member who harmed you is in a union — for example, an AAUP chapter — they have collectively bargained due-process rights that can lengthen the discipline timeline. This does not stop your Title IX case. It does sometimes mean discipline takes longer than you expect. The Title IX office should explain how their union contract interacts with the case.

tiles.label: Talk confidentially first
tiles.subtitle: No investigation triggered
tiles.spokenText: Before deciding whether to formally report, you can talk to a confidential resource — a counselor, CARE advocate, or off-campus advocate. Nothing will trigger an investigation. They can help you sort through your options.

tiles.label: Title IX outside attorney
tiles.subtitle: Free consultation
tiles.spokenText: Some organizations provide free consultations for student survivors of faculty misconduct: Know Your IX, the Title IX Defense Coalition, and survivor-side firms listed by SurvJustice. They can advise you on your options before you commit to a path.

tiles.label: Stalking — pattern of unwanted contact
tiles.spokenText: Stalking — pattern of unwanted contact

tiles.label: Stalking is a crime
tiles.subtitle: You can document + report
tiles.spokenText: Stalking is a pattern of repeated, unwanted contact that makes you fear for your safety or emotional well-being. Stalking is a crime under Connecticut state law (and is also criminalized under federal interstate-stalking statute 18 U.S.C. 2261A). On the campus side: the Violence Against Women Act amendments to Clery — Campus SaVE — give you specific rights and reporting protections on campus, including no-contact orders and supportive measures. The pattern matters more than any single incident. Documenting the pattern is the most important thing you can do.

tiles.label: They are here NOW
tiles.subtitle: Active threat
tiles.spokenText: The stalker is on campus right now and I am afraid. Please call campus police or 911 immediately.

tiles.label: Document the pattern
tiles.subtitle: Save everything
tiles.spokenText: Document every contact: screenshots of texts and DMs, time-stamped notes of in-person sightings, photos of gifts or letters, voicemails saved as audio files, witness names. Save metadata — do not delete or forward. The pattern is your case.

tiles.label: Stalker is a STUDENT
tiles.subtitle: Title IX + campus conduct
tiles.spokenText: If the stalker is a current or former student, you can file both a Title IX complaint (stalking is covered) and a campus code-of-conduct report. The school can issue a no-contact order and supportive measures even before any investigation.

tiles.label: Stalker is FACULTY / STAFF
tiles.subtitle: Power-dynamic path
tiles.spokenText: If the stalker is a faculty member or staff, the power-dynamic Title IX path applies. Supportive measures can include reassignment so you do not have to interact with them academically.

tiles.label: Stalker is NOT affiliated
tiles.subtitle: Criminal path + protective order
tiles.spokenText: If the stalker is not a student, employee, or affiliate of the campus, the primary path is criminal report plus civil protective order. The campus can still help with safety measures on campus.

tiles.label: Apply for protective order
tiles.subtitle: CT court process
tiles.spokenText: In Connecticut, you can apply for a civil restraining order from Family Court if the stalker is a current or former intimate partner, or a civil protection order from Superior Court if they are not. The form is called CV-1 or JD-FM-137. You can also ask law enforcement for a temporary order via your criminal report. The CT Coalition Against Domestic Violence advocate line is 1-888-774-2900.

tiles.label: Cyber-stalking (online)
tiles.subtitle: Block + report platforms
tiles.spokenText: For online stalking: block the person on every platform, report their accounts (Meta, Instagram, Snapchat, Discord, TikTok, Twitter/X all have report-for-stalking flows), enable two-factor authentication everywhere, change your passwords, lock down location sharing. Do NOT delete the messages — screenshot them first.

tiles.label: Sextortion · revenge porn · deepfakes
tiles.spokenText: Sextortion · revenge porn · deepfakes

tiles.label: You are not alone — this is a crime
tiles.subtitle: Not your fault
tiles.spokenText: Sextortion, revenge porn, and AI deepfake abuse are crimes. They are happening to college students every day. None of this is your fault. There is a clear path to take.

tiles.label: DO NOT DELETE the messages
tiles.subtitle: They are evidence
tiles.spokenText: Important: do NOT delete the threats, messages, or images. They are evidence. Take screenshots that include the username, the date, and the platform. Save the original messages too. The metadata helps investigators.

tiles.label: Screenshot everything
tiles.subtitle: Include username + timestamps
tiles.spokenText: For each piece of evidence: screenshot the conversation showing the username, the date, and the message text. Also save the original message thread. If possible, record the URL of the profile.

tiles.label: DO NOT PAY the extortionist
tiles.subtitle: FBI guidance
tiles.spokenText: If someone is threatening to release intimate images unless you pay or send more images, do NOT pay or send anything. The FBI says paying almost always leads to more demands, not the end of the threat. Stop the conversation, save the evidence, and report.

tiles.label: I am in crisis — 988
tiles.subtitle: Mental health priority
tiles.spokenText: Sextortion victims have a very high suicide risk. If you are in mental-health crisis right now, please call or text 988. You are worth so much more than this. The crisis line counselors are trained for this exact situation.

tiles.label: Were you under 18 in the image?
tiles.subtitle: CSAM — different + faster process
tiles.spokenText: If you were under eighteen years old when the images were made — even if you are eighteen or older now — this is child sexual abuse material under federal law. Two free services exist specifically for this: NCMEC TakeItDown at takeitdown.ncmec.org, and Cybertipline. They work directly with platforms to remove the imagery. Free, confidential.

tiles.label: FBI cyber crime report — IC3
tiles.subtitle: Federal level
tiles.spokenText: The FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center — IC3 — at ic3.gov accepts cyber crime reports including sextortion. The FBI has a dedicated sextortion task force. You can also call your local FBI office.

tiles.label: CCRI 24/7 helpline
tiles.subtitle: Cyber Civil Rights Initiative
tiles.spokenText: The Cyber Civil Rights Initiative — CCRI — runs a twenty-four hour helpline specifically for victims of image-based sexual abuse. Phone 1-844-878-2274. Free, confidential, with trained counselors and platform-takedown help.

tiles.label: Report on platforms
tiles.subtitle: IG / Snap / Discord / TikTok
tiles.spokenText: Every major platform has a specific report flow for non-consensual intimate imagery. Instagram and Facebook: settings, help, report a problem, intimate images. Snapchat: report and then choose harassment then nudity. Discord and TikTok: trust and safety. Twitter/X: report tweet then non-consensual nudity. Save your report ticket numbers.

tiles.label: AI deepfake of me
tiles.subtitle: Synthetic intimate imagery
tiles.spokenText: If someone made an AI deepfake intimate image of you without your consent, it is non-consensual intimate imagery under most state laws including Connecticut's revenge-porn statute. NCMEC TakeItDown also handles deepfakes when the subject was under eighteen when the source images were taken.

tiles.label: Perpetrator is a student
tiles.subtitle: Title IX too
tiles.spokenText: If the person sharing the images is a current student, the campus Title IX office can investigate this as sexual harassment under Title IX, in addition to the criminal report.

tiles.label: Hazing — coerced activity to join
tiles.spokenText: Hazing — coerced activity to join

tiles.label: Hazing is illegal
tiles.subtitle: CT state law + Clery Act
tiles.spokenText: Hazing is illegal under Connecticut state law. The federal Stop Campus Hazing Act, signed December 23, 2024, requires schools to publicly report hazing incidents in three ways: (a) publish a Campus Hazing Transparency Report on their website, updated at least twice per year; (b) publish their hazing policy publicly; and (c) include hazing in their annual Clery security reports. Hazing can include forcing someone to consume alcohol or drugs, physical abuse, humiliation, sleep deprivation, isolation, or any activity that causes physical or psychological harm — even if the person says they agreed. Coercion is not consent.

tiles.label: MEDICAL EMERGENCY now
tiles.subtitle: Alcohol poisoning / injury
tiles.spokenText: Someone needs medical attention right now from a hazing-related activity. Please call 911 immediately. Most colleges have a medical amnesty policy — calling for help does NOT get you in trouble for underage drinking or drug use. The life matters more than any conduct rule.

tiles.label: It is happening right now
tiles.subtitle: Active situation
tiles.spokenText: Hazing is happening right now. Please contact campus police or 911 immediately. The activity must stop before someone is hurt.

tiles.label: Anonymous report
tiles.subtitle: 888-NOT-HAZE national hotline
tiles.spokenText: The national Anti-Hazing Hotline at 1-888-NOT-HAZE — that is 1-888-668-4293 — accepts anonymous reports about hazing at any campus. They forward the report to the relevant national fraternity or sorority headquarters and to the campus. You can report without giving your name.

tiles.label: Greek life (fraternity / sorority)
tiles.subtitle: National + campus paths
tiles.spokenText: If hazing is happening in a fraternity or sorority, you can report to BOTH the campus office for Fraternity and Sorority Life AND the national headquarters of that organization. National often has more authority to suspend or close a chapter. The Anti-Hazing Hotline routes both ways automatically.

tiles.label: Athletic team
tiles.subtitle: Athletics dept + Title IX
tiles.spokenText: If hazing is happening on an athletic team, the campus Athletics department has authority to suspend or remove players and coaches. NCAA also has anti-hazing policy. If the hazing involved sexual content, Title IX applies too.

tiles.label: Club / org / military
tiles.subtitle: Student activities + Dean
tiles.spokenText: If hazing is in a club or student organization, the Office of Student Activities and the Dean of Students can investigate and remove club recognition. For ROTC or military programs, the unit commanding officer is the right reporting path.

tiles.label: Hazing involved sexual content
tiles.subtitle: Title IX path also
tiles.spokenText: If the hazing involved sexual touching, forced exposure, or any sexual activity, this is sexual misconduct under Title IX in addition to hazing. Both paths can run at the same time.

tiles.label: I was made to participate
tiles.subtitle: You are not in trouble
tiles.spokenText: If you were the one being hazed and you were made to do things you regret — including hazing newer members later — that is how hazing works. Coercion under threat of being kicked out is not the same as voluntary participation. Connecticut's anti-hazing statute and many campus policies include provisions intended to protect victims who later participated under coercion — ask the Dean of Students how the policy applies to your situation. Confidential support is available regardless of how the conduct office classifies you.

tiles.label: Bias incident — identity-based harm
tiles.spokenText: Bias incident — identity-based harm

tiles.label: What a bias incident is
tiles.subtitle: Different from a hate crime
tiles.spokenText: A bias incident is when someone targets you because of your race, religion, national origin, disability, sexual orientation, gender identity, immigration status, or other identity. It may not rise to the level of a criminal hate crime — but it still harms you and the campus community. Documentation matters even if no criminal charges are filed. The campus uses bias-incident reports to track climate and respond to patterns.

tiles.label: Active threat right now
tiles.spokenText: If you are in immediate danger or being threatened right now, please call campus police or 911.

tiles.label: I was physically hurt
tiles.subtitle: Hate crime — criminal report
tiles.spokenText: If the bias incident involved physical violence, threats with a weapon, or property destruction, it may be a hate crime under federal or Connecticut law. You can file both a criminal report (campus police or town police) AND a bias-incident report on campus. Both can run at the same time.

tiles.label: Verbal slur or threat
tiles.subtitle: Document the words
tiles.spokenText: Write down what was said as exactly as you can remember, when, where, and any witnesses. Even if you cannot remember word-for-word, write down the gist and what you felt.

tiles.label: Online harassment
tiles.subtitle: Screenshot everything
tiles.spokenText: For online bias incidents: screenshot the messages or posts, save the username and URL, save the timestamp. Then report on the platform AND to the campus bias-incident system.

tiles.label: Graffiti / physical signs
tiles.subtitle: Photo + location
tiles.spokenText: For graffiti or physical bias incidents: take a photo, note the exact location, the time you found it, and any witnesses. Then contact campus facilities to document before removal, and the bias-incident team.

tiles.label: Campus bias-incident report
tiles.subtitle: Online form usually
tiles.spokenText: Most campuses have a dedicated bias-incident report form online — often called Bias Incident Response Team, BIRT, or Office of Institutional Equity. You can usually report anonymously. The form goes to a small team that investigates and supports the targets of the incident.

tiles.label: Office of Institutional Equity and Accessibility (OIEA) — University Title IX Office
tiles.subtitle: MANDATORY REPORTER · 82-90 Wall Street · 203-432-6854
tiles.spokenText: WARNING: This office is a mandatory reporter. If you tell them what happened, they are required to notify the school. Office of Institutional Equity and Accessibility (OIEA) — University Title IX Office. Address: 82-90 Wall Street, 4th Floor, New Haven, CT 06511. Phone: 203-432-6854.

tiles.label: Federal complaint — Title VI
tiles.subtitle: Race, color, national origin
tiles.spokenText: If the bias is based on race, color, or national origin, you can file a separate complaint with the federal Department of Education Office for Civil Rights — OCR. Title VI applies to any institution that receives federal funds. The complaint can be filed online at ocrcas.ed.gov.

tiles.label: Federal complaint — ADA / 504
tiles.subtitle: Disability-based bias
tiles.spokenText: If the bias is disability-based, you can also file with the Department of Education OCR under Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act and the Americans with Disabilities Act.

tiles.label: Identity-specific advocacy
tiles.subtitle: NAACP / ADL / GLAAD / etc.
tiles.spokenText: Identity-specific civil rights organizations can support you: NAACP for race-based incidents, ADL for antisemitism, GLAAD for LGBTQ+ incidents, MALDEF for Latino civil rights, NQAPIA for queer Asian/Pacific Islander, CAIR for anti-Muslim incidents. They can advocate on your behalf and connect you with legal help.

tiles.label: Yale SHARE Center (Sexual Harassment and Assault Response & Education)
tiles.subtitle: Confidential · Yale Health Building · 203-432-2000
tiles.spokenText: This office is confidential. What you tell them stays private, unless there is a narrow safety or legal exception. Yale SHARE Center (Sexual Harassment and Assault Response & Education). Address: Yale Health Building, Lower Level, 55 Lock Street, New Haven, CT 06511. Phone: 203-432-2000.

tiles.label: Talk to a counselor
tiles.subtitle: Identity-affirming therapy if available
tiles.spokenText: Bias incidents are traumatic. I want to talk to a counselor — ideally one who is identity-affirming for me.

tiles.label: Code-of-conduct violation accused
tiles.spokenText: Code-of-conduct violation accused

tiles.label: You have procedural rights
tiles.subtitle: Read before you talk
tiles.spokenText: If you have been notified that you are accused of a code-of-conduct violation, you have specific procedural rights. Important: do NOT have any conversation about the incident with the investigator, the complainant, or witnesses without first understanding your options. Anything you say can become part of the record.

tiles.label: Is this a Title IX matter?
tiles.subtitle: Sexual misconduct allegation
tiles.spokenText: If you have been notified that you are accused of sexual harassment, sexual assault, dating violence, domestic violence, or stalking, you are in the Title IX process — which has its own procedures. You have the right to a written notice of allegations, an advisor (including a lawyer), cross-examination at a live hearing, presumption of non-responsibility, and a written decision with reasoning. Ask the Title IX office for the written rules.

tiles.label: You can bring an advisor
tiles.subtitle: Including a lawyer in some cases
tiles.spokenText: You have the right to bring an advisor to any meeting or hearing. For Title IX hearings, this is required to include a lawyer if you choose. For other code-of-conduct matters, the advisor is often a campus student-advocate or someone you trust. Ask the conduct office for their rules on advisors.

tiles.label: Get the charges IN WRITING
tiles.subtitle: Before any meeting
tiles.spokenText: You have the right to a written notice that specifies exactly which rules you are accused of violating, the date and location of the alleged incident, and the basic facts. Do NOT meet with the investigator until you have read the written charges and any evidence they have shared with you.

tiles.label: Document your side
tiles.subtitle: Save everything
tiles.spokenText: Before any meeting, write down your own account of the incident in detail — dates, times, who was there, what you remember. Save any messages, photos, or other evidence. Make a list of witnesses on your behalf. The earlier you write it down, the more credible it is.

tiles.label: Don't contact complainant / witnesses
tiles.subtitle: Can be retaliation
tiles.spokenText: Do NOT reach out to the person who complained about you, or to potential witnesses, to discuss the case. This can be considered retaliation, which is itself a code-of-conduct violation — even if the original complaint is dismissed. Talk only through your advisor.

tiles.label: Student Legal Services
tiles.subtitle: Free advice on campus
tiles.spokenText: Many campuses have a Student Legal Services office that provides free consultation for students facing conduct charges. They are NOT the same as the Dean of Students or Title IX — they are advocates for you, the student. Look in the student handbook or ask the Dean of Students office for the contact.

tiles.label: Campus Ombudsperson
tiles.subtitle: Confidential, informal
tiles.spokenText: A campus ombudsperson — if your campus has one — provides confidential, informal advice on navigating conduct processes. They are neutral; they will not advocate for you against the school, but they can explain your rights and the process.

tiles.label: FIRE — Foundation for Individual Rights
tiles.subtitle: Free help for accused students
tiles.spokenText: The Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression — FIRE — at thefire.org provides free guidance and sometimes legal representation for students accused of conduct violations, especially in free-speech and due-process cases. Their case-submission form is on their website.

tiles.label: International student?
tiles.subtitle: Visa-status implications
tiles.spokenText: If you are an international student on F-1 or J-1 status, a conduct suspension longer than five months can trigger automatic SEVIS termination. Even a finding of responsibility without suspension can affect future visa applications. Talk to your International Student Services office BEFORE the hearing.

tiles.label: Financial aid implications
tiles.subtitle: Conduct suspension can void Title IV
tiles.spokenText: A conduct suspension can also affect your federal financial aid. Drug-related convictions during an aid period historically affected eligibility (the FAFSA question was removed in 2021 but some states still penalize). A finding does not automatically disqualify aid — but you should know the rules. Talk to financial aid BEFORE the hearing.

tiles.label: Office of the Dean of Yale College
tiles.subtitle: 1 Hillhouse Avenue · 203-432-2900
tiles.spokenText: Office of the Dean of Yale College. Address: 1 Hillhouse Avenue, New Haven, CT 06511. Phone: 203-432-2900.

tiles.label: Read the appeals policy NOW
tiles.subtitle: Before you need it
tiles.spokenText: The conduct office must have a written appeals policy. Read it before your hearing so you know the timeline — usually you have five to fourteen days after the decision to file an appeal. Common appeal grounds: procedural error, new evidence not previously available, or sanction grossly disproportionate to the violation. Save the policy.

tiles.label: Talk to a counselor
tiles.subtitle: Conduct cases are stressful
tiles.spokenText: Being accused is stressful and can affect your sleep, focus, and grades. I want to talk to a counselor confidentially.

tiles.label: Academic integrity charge — plagiarism
tiles.spokenText: Academic integrity charge — plagiarism

tiles.label: Take this seriously
tiles.subtitle: Plus: you have rights
tiles.spokenText: A plagiarism accusation is serious and can result in a failing grade, course failure, suspension, or expulsion at the highest sanction levels. But you also have due-process rights, including a fair hearing and an appeal. Do not panic. Do not admit to anything before you have understood the full situation.

tiles.label: Ask for the evidence in writing
tiles.subtitle: Specific passages alleged
tiles.spokenText: Ask your professor or the honor council to show you in writing: which specific passages of your work are alleged to be plagiarized, and from what source. You cannot defend yourself without knowing exactly what is being challenged. You have the right to this information.

tiles.label: Preserve YOUR evidence
tiles.subtitle: Drafts, version history, sources
tiles.spokenText: Save everything that shows your writing process: earlier drafts of the paper, Google Docs or Word version history, your notes, the sources you actually used, browser history showing your research, any emails with the professor or TA. The most effective defense in a plagiarism case is showing your authentic process.

tiles.label: Google Docs version history
tiles.subtitle: Critical for defense
tiles.spokenText: If you wrote in Google Docs: open the document, click File, then Version History, then See Version History. This shows the entire timeline of your writing — every keystroke, every edit. This is among the strongest evidence you can show. Take a screen recording or screenshots of the version history before anything changes.

tiles.label: Microsoft Word track changes
tiles.subtitle: Document metadata
tiles.spokenText: If you wrote in Microsoft Word: the document metadata (File menu, Properties, Statistics) shows total editing time and revision count. If track changes was enabled, your full edit history is there. Preserve the original file — do not edit it before the hearing.

tiles.label: Why am I being accused?
tiles.subtitle: Common reasons
tiles.spokenText: Common reasons for a plagiarism accusation: (1) Turnitin or similar tool flagged similarity to existing sources, often false-positively due to common phrases or properly-cited quotes. (2) Self-plagiarism — submitting your own past work without disclosure. (3) Missing or incorrect citation of a source you DID use. (4) Paraphrasing too close to the original. Each has a different defense strategy.

tiles.label: Wait — is this about AI?
tiles.subtitle: Different defense
tiles.spokenText: If you are accused of using generative AI like ChatGPT or Claude in your work, that is a different category from plagiarism in the traditional sense. AI-use accusations have their own defense strategy.

tiles.label: Bring an advisor
tiles.subtitle: Trusted faculty or student
tiles.spokenText: Most academic-integrity processes allow you to bring an advisor — usually a trusted faculty member, a student-advocate from Student Legal Services, or sometimes a lawyer. Ask the honor council or your dean about their advisor rules.

tiles.label: Honor council process
tiles.subtitle: Hearing + appeal
tiles.spokenText: Most institutions handle academic integrity through an Honor Council or similar body. You should receive a written notice of charges, an opportunity for a hearing where you present your side, and a written decision with reasoning. There is usually an appeal path. Read the policy in your student handbook.

tiles.label: Accused of using ChatGPT / Claude / Gemini
tiles.spokenText: Accused of using ChatGPT / Claude / Gemini

tiles.label: AI-detection tools are unreliable
tiles.subtitle: Real research backs this up
tiles.spokenText: Important context: AI-detection tools like Turnitin AI detection, GPTZero, and Originality.ai have published false-positive rates between five and twenty percent. Stanford research has shown them to systematically flag work by non-native English speakers as AI-generated even when it is not. OpenAI shut down its own AI-detection tool in 2023 because of accuracy concerns. The tool flagged you, but the tool is not reliable. This is a defensible accusation.

tiles.label: Ask what detector + what threshold
tiles.subtitle: Specific evidence in writing
tiles.spokenText: Ask your professor or honor council: which AI-detection tool flagged the work, what score it returned, what is the threshold for the accusation. Document this. AI-detection tools should NEVER be the sole basis for an academic-integrity finding — that has been formal policy at many institutions including some MIT departments, Vanderbilt, and others.

tiles.label: Show your process
tiles.subtitle: Drafts + version history + sources
tiles.spokenText: The strongest defense against an AI-use accusation is showing your authentic writing process. Save and preserve: Google Docs version history (File > Version History), Word document revisions, your handwritten or typed notes, browser history of research, any voice-memo brainstorms, photos of your whiteboard or notebook drafts. Real human writing has revisions, false starts, and a timeline. AI output does not.

tiles.label: Screen-record your writing
tiles.subtitle: For future assignments
tiles.spokenText: Going forward, you can protect yourself by screen-recording yourself writing important papers in Google Docs. The recording shows your real-time editing process — the strongest possible proof that you wrote the work. Free tools like Loom, OBS Studio, or QuickTime work for this.

tiles.label: Common false-positive triggers
tiles.subtitle: Things that fool detectors
tiles.spokenText: AI-detection tools commonly false-positive on: writing by non-native English speakers, writing on technical or scientific topics (because AI has memorized them), use of common transitional phrases, writing that is highly polished, writing that follows a clear five-paragraph essay structure, and writing that uses sources the detector also references. None of these mean you used AI — they mean the detector is bad.

tiles.label: I did use AI for SOME of it
tiles.subtitle: Honest disclosure may help
tiles.spokenText: If you did use AI for part of the work — say, for brainstorming, outlining, or grammar checking, but not the actual writing — many institutions have moved toward a disclosure model rather than zero-tolerance. Honest disclosure of what you used and how, before the hearing, can often result in a lesser sanction than denial-then-finding-of-responsibility. Talk to a student advocate first.

tiles.label: Bring an advisor
tiles.subtitle: Trusted faculty / Student Legal
tiles.spokenText: You have the right to bring an advisor to any hearing — usually a trusted faculty member, a Student Legal Services advocate, or a lawyer.

tiles.label: FIRE — due-process resources
tiles.subtitle: Free guidance for accused students
tiles.spokenText: The Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression — FIRE — at thefire.org publishes guidance and resources for students facing campus due-process challenges. Some of their materials specifically address AI-detection and academic-integrity defense. They have a case-submission form for students who need direct help.

pool.title: I Am Worried About a Friend

tiles.label: Friend in crisis — you noticed something
tiles.spokenText: Friend in crisis — you noticed something

tiles.label: Reaching out is the right thing
tiles.subtitle: You are not breaking their trust
tiles.spokenText: Reaching out for a friend in crisis is one of the most important things you can do. It is not breaking their trust to ask for help — it is keeping them alive. The school has people whose entire job is to respond to friend-of-concern reports without scaring or punishing the friend.

tiles.label: They are in IMMEDIATE danger
tiles.subtitle: Self-harm / overdose / threat
tiles.spokenText: My friend is in immediate danger right now — actively attempting self-harm, has overdosed, or is in a violent situation. Call 911 immediately. Stay on the phone with them or with 911 until help arrives if you can.

tiles.label: They mentioned suicide
tiles.subtitle: 988 — call or text
tiles.spokenText: My friend has talked about wanting to die or has shared a plan to hurt themselves. Call or text 988 — the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. You can call WITH them, or call FOR them if they cannot. The counselors are trained for this exact situation.

tiles.label: CARE team / behavioral concern report
tiles.subtitle: Not emergency — coordinated response
tiles.spokenText: Many campuses have a CARE team — sometimes called Behavioral Intervention Team (BIT), Students of Concern, or similar — that responds to non-emergency friend-of-concern reports. They coordinate outreach across counseling, housing, academic advising, and the Dean of Students. Outreach is often by a counselor rather than police, but the specific response depends on the school and the situation. You can usually submit an online form. Ask the Dean of Students if you cannot find the form.

tiles.label: What to include
tiles.subtitle: Specific behaviors observed
tiles.spokenText: In your CARE report or conversation with the dean, include: specific behaviors you observed (not labels — describe what you saw or heard), when and where, who else was there, what your friend said directly if anything, your relationship to them, what you have already tried, and what you fear could happen.

tiles.label: Substance abuse concern
tiles.subtitle: Medical amnesty applies
tiles.spokenText: If your friend is using drugs or drinking dangerously, most campuses have a medical amnesty policy — calling for help does NOT get either of you in conduct trouble. Use it. The student health center and CARE team can coordinate a substance-use evaluation without involving police.

tiles.label: Eating disorder concern
tiles.subtitle: Health center + CAPS
tiles.spokenText: Eating disorders often start in college. If your friend is showing signs — sudden weight changes, food rituals, secrecy around eating, comments about hating their body — the student health center and CAPS work together on this. NEDA (National Eating Disorders Association) helpline is 1-800-931-2237.

tiles.label: Friend is isolating / depressed
tiles.subtitle: CARE outreach
tiles.spokenText: If your friend has been withdrawing, not eating, skipping classes, sleeping all the time, or seems hopeless — these can be signs of major depression. A CARE-team check-in can be the bridge. CARE outreach often aims for supportive outreach, not a punishment — but the specific response depends on the school and situation.

tiles.label: Friend in abusive relationship
tiles.subtitle: DV-aware response
tiles.spokenText: If your friend is in a relationship where their partner is controlling, isolating, monitoring, or hurting them, the campus has confidential domestic-violence advocates. CT CCADV at 1-888-774-2900 has trained advocates. The Title IX office can also help if both people are students. Approach your friend gently — never confront the partner.

tiles.label: Friend in cult / coercive group
tiles.subtitle: ICSA + chaplain + CAPS
tiles.spokenText: If your friend has gotten involved with a group that is isolating them from family or controlling their behavior — religious cult, multi-level marketing, extremist political group — the International Cultic Studies Association at ICSA-home.com has specific resources. Many campus chaplaincies have experience here too.

tiles.subtitle: 1 Hillhouse Avenue · 203-432-2900
tiles.spokenText: Office of the Dean of Yale College. Address: 1 Hillhouse Avenue, New Haven, CT 06511. Phone: 203-432-2900.

tiles.spokenText: Yale Mental Health & Counseling (YMHC). Address: 55 Lock Street, 3rd Floor, New Haven, CT 06520. Phone: 203-432-0290.

tiles.label: I need support too
tiles.subtitle: Caring is exhausting
tiles.spokenText: Being the friend who notices and reaches out is exhausting. You also deserve support. Many counseling centers offer specific groups or sessions for students who are supporting a friend in crisis.

tiles.label: Cannot reach them — want someone to check
tiles.spokenText: Cannot reach them — want someone to check

tiles.label: What a welfare check is
tiles.subtitle: Read before you request
tiles.spokenText: A welfare check is when you ask law enforcement or campus staff to physically visit someone you are worried about. Important: in some cases — especially for people with trauma around police, mental-illness history, or non-citizen status — a police welfare check can make things worse. Read the options carefully. There are alternatives.

tiles.label: They might be seriously hurt NOW
tiles.spokenText: If you believe your friend is in immediate physical danger — actively attempting suicide, having a medical emergency, in a violent situation — call 911. This is the fastest response. Give the address and explain what you fear.

tiles.label: They live ON campus
tiles.subtitle: Campus PD knows the buildings
tiles.spokenText: If your friend lives in a campus residence hall, campus police is usually faster and more familiar with the building than town police. They can also coordinate with the Resident Director and Resident Assistant. Tell them: the room number, your relationship, what specifically you are worried about.

tiles.label: Yale Police Department (YPD)
tiles.subtitle: 101 Ashmun Street · 203-432-4400
tiles.spokenText: Yale Police Department (YPD). Address: 101 Ashmun Street, New Haven, CT 06511. Phone: 203-432-4400.

tiles.label: They live OFF campus
tiles.subtitle: Town police in their town
tiles.spokenText: If your friend lives off campus, call the local police in the town where they live — non-emergency line. Look up the number for the town's police department. Give them the address, your relationship, what specifically you are worried about, and that you are requesting a welfare check.

tiles.label: Mobile crisis (NOT police)
tiles.subtitle: CT 988 mobile response
tiles.spokenText: In Connecticut, 988 can connect you to mobile-crisis services or transfer your call to a local mobile-crisis team when the concern is mental-health-related and not immediately physically dangerous. Mobile-crisis teams include mental-health clinicians, not officers. This is often a safer first response for someone with trauma history. Tell 988: I am asking about a mobile-crisis response for a friend in mental-health crisis, not a police welfare check. The 988 counselor will tell you what is available right now in their area.

tiles.label: What to tell the responder
tiles.subtitle: Important information
tiles.spokenText: When you request a welfare check, give: your friend's name, age, address, last contact you had with them and when, what specifically concerns you (be specific — depression for two weeks, suicidal text yesterday, has not answered for three days), whether they have access to firearms or medications they could overdose on, any mental-health diagnoses or medications, your relationship to them, your contact information for follow-up.

tiles.label: About involuntary hold (PEC / 7-day)
tiles.subtitle: Know before you call
tiles.spokenText: In Connecticut, a Police Emergency Certificate (PEC) allows police to transport someone to an emergency room for psychiatric evaluation if they appear to be in immediate danger to self or others. From there, a clinician decides whether to admit involuntarily for up to fifteen days. For some friends — especially those with prior negative hospital experiences or trauma — this can be more harmful than helpful. Ask 988 about voluntary alternatives first if there is time.

tiles.label: Follow up afterward
tiles.subtitle: Stay engaged
tiles.spokenText: After the welfare check, follow up: call your friend if they are willing to talk, ask the campus CARE team to do an outreach, check on them again in a few days. A welfare check is one moment in time. Real support is showing up over time.

tiles.label: Take care of yourself too
tiles.spokenText: Worrying about a friend like this is exhausting. I want to talk to a counselor for myself.

tiles.spokenText: Go back

tiles.spokenText: Take me back to the main screen.

tiles.label: Death of someone close — what to do
tiles.spokenText: Death of someone close — what to do

tiles.label: I'm so sorry for your loss
tiles.subtitle: Take this one step at a time
tiles.spokenText: I am so sorry for your loss. The school will work with you on academics and practical matters — you do not have to handle this alone. The most important thing right now is taking care of yourself. The kiosk will help you navigate the offices you need.

tiles.label: Death in immediate family
tiles.subtitle: Parent / sibling / spouse
tiles.spokenText: Most schools offer a bereavement absence policy for the death of a parent, sibling, spouse, or child — typically three to five business days excused, sometimes longer for travel. Contact the Dean of Students FIRST — they notify all your professors at once so you do not have to email each one.

tiles.label: Death of a friend / classmate
tiles.subtitle: Often missed
tiles.spokenText: The loss of a close friend or classmate is often not formally covered by bereavement policy — but the Dean of Students can still help you arrange short-term absence and connect you with grief support. Ask them, do not assume.

tiles.label: Death of a faculty member
tiles.subtitle: Campus-wide impact
tiles.spokenText: If a faculty member has died, the school usually arranges memorial services and grief support. The CAPS office will often offer drop-in grief groups. You are not alone in the loss.

tiles.label: Suicide loss specifically
tiles.subtitle: Unique grief — special groups
tiles.spokenText: Loss to suicide has its own kind of grief — guilt, anger, why questions that may never have answers. The American Foundation for Suicide Prevention runs survivors-of-suicide-loss groups at afsp.org. CAPS often has a dedicated grief group too. Talk to a counselor specifically trained in suicide-loss grief if possible.

tiles.label: Office of the Dean of Yale College
tiles.subtitle: 1 Hillhouse Avenue · 203-432-2900
tiles.spokenText: Office of the Dean of Yale College. Address: 1 Hillhouse Avenue, New Haven, CT 06511. Phone: 203-432-2900.

tiles.label: Dean coordinates professors
tiles.subtitle: One email to them, they tell everyone
tiles.spokenText: The Dean of Students office can often send a notification on your behalf to all your professors saying you have had a death in the family. Many schools use this to spare you having to write the same email five times. Confirm the process at your school. They are also the ones who arrange exam postponements and extensions when granted.

tiles.label: Yale Mental Health & Counseling (YMHC)
tiles.subtitle: 55 Lock Street · 203-432-0290
tiles.spokenText: Yale Mental Health & Counseling (YMHC). Address: 55 Lock Street, 3rd Floor, New Haven, CT 06520. Phone: 203-432-0290.

tiles.label: Religious / chaplaincy
tiles.subtitle: If meaningful for you
tiles.spokenText: If your faith tradition matters to you, the campus chaplaincy office usually has chaplains across denominations and can support grieving rituals, funerals, or memorial services. They are also confidential.

tiles.label: I need to leave school for a while
tiles.subtitle: Medical withdrawal path
tiles.spokenText: Many schools allow grief to support a medical or personal withdrawal — talk to the Dean of Students about which category fits at this school. A medical withdrawal, when granted, can preserve your good standing and protect financial aid in ways a regular withdrawal does not — but it is not automatic and not every school has the same rules. Ask first.

tiles.label: Financial aid + withdrawal
tiles.subtitle: Check before you leave
tiles.spokenText: If you do withdraw, federal financial aid rules can require repayment of aid disbursed earlier in the term. Medical withdrawal often has better outcomes than regular withdrawal here. Check with financial aid before you decide, OR ask the Dean of Students to coordinate the conversation for you.

tiles.label: I am in crisis from this loss
tiles.subtitle: 988 / counselor now
tiles.spokenText: Grief can be a mental-health crisis. If you are having thoughts of harming yourself, call or text 988. There is no shame in this. Loss can break us. Counselors trained in grief and crisis are here.

tiles.label: Long-term grief support
tiles.subtitle: GriefShare + AFSP + Soaring Spirits
tiles.spokenText: For long-term grief support beyond the school: GriefShare at griefshare.org runs faith-based grief groups. AFSP at afsp.org for suicide loss. Soaring Spirits International for widow / widower support. Many of these are free.

pool.title: I Have No Safe Place Tonight

tiles.label: Emergency housing — same-day need
tiles.spokenText: Emergency housing — same-day need

tiles.label: You will not be alone tonight
tiles.subtitle: There are options — let me help
tiles.spokenText: You will not be alone tonight. There are emergency-housing options. Some are right on campus, some are off campus. The kiosk will help you find the right one for your situation.

tiles.label: Fleeing abuse / violence
tiles.subtitle: Confidential DV shelter path
tiles.spokenText: If you are leaving an abusive partner, family member, or housemate, the campus knows how to keep your new location confidential. Call the CT Coalition Against Domestic Violence at 1-888-774-2900 — they have shelter beds across CT and can also help with safety planning. The campus Title IX office can help if the abuser is a student.

tiles.label: Fire / flood / building damage
tiles.subtitle: Campus emergency relocation
tiles.spokenText: If your dorm or apartment is damaged by fire, flood, or other emergency, the campus Residence Life office has emergency-relocation procedures. Call campus residence life or campus police — they will arrange a temporary room. Red Cross also helps with clothing, food, and supplies after a fire.

tiles.label: Locked out after hours
tiles.subtitle: RA / RD chain
tiles.spokenText: For after-hours lockout from your dorm, contact your RA — Resident Assistant — first. They have access to the on-call Resident Director who can let you in or issue a temporary key. Most campuses charge a small fee for an after-hours lockout — many waive it for the first one.

tiles.label: Kicked out of family home
tiles.subtitle: Family rejected me — common for LGBTQ+
tiles.spokenText: If your family has rejected you — sometimes for being LGBTQ+, sometimes for other reasons — the Dean of Students office often has emergency-grant funds for temporary housing, and can connect you with on-campus emergency rooms or off-campus partner shelters. CT 211 also has a youth/young-adult specific pathway.

tiles.label: Eviction / financial crisis
tiles.subtitle: CT 211 housing
tiles.spokenText: If you are being evicted from an off-campus apartment, call CT 211 immediately — they triage same-day. CT has eviction-prevention funds and emergency rental assistance. Press 1 for housing and follow the menu.

tiles.label: CT 211 — call right now
tiles.subtitle: Statewide info-and-referral
tiles.spokenText: Connecticut 2-1-1. Dial 2-1-1 from any phone in CT. Free, twenty-four hours. They help find emergency shelter beds, eviction help, food assistance, utility help — they are the central referral point.

tiles.label: NDVH — 1-800-799-7233
tiles.subtitle: 24/7 DV
tiles.spokenText: National Domestic Violence Hotline. 1-800-799-7233. They will route you to a CT-specific shelter if you are fleeing abuse.

tiles.label: National Runaway Safeline
tiles.subtitle: For under 21 — 1-800-RUNAWAY
tiles.spokenText: If you are under twenty-one and have left an unsafe family situation, the National Runaway Safeline at 1-800-786-2929 connects to emergency shelters that specialize in serving young adults.

tiles.label: True Colors United (LGBTQ+ youth)
tiles.subtitle: LGBTQ+ housing focus
tiles.spokenText: True Colors United focuses specifically on LGBTQ+ young people experiencing homelessness. They partner with shelters that are safe and affirming. Find their resources at truecolorsunited.org.

tiles.subtitle: 1 Hillhouse Avenue · 203-432-2900
tiles.spokenText: Office of the Dean of Yale College. Address: 1 Hillhouse Avenue, New Haven, CT 06511. Phone: 203-432-2900.

tiles.subtitle: 101 Ashmun Street · 203-432-4400
tiles.spokenText: Yale Police Department (YPD). Address: 101 Ashmun Street, New Haven, CT 06511. Phone: 203-432-4400.

tiles.label: I'm hungry / need supplies too
tiles.subtitle: Food pantry + emergency grant
tiles.spokenText: Most campuses have a student food pantry — usually free, no questions asked. The Dean of Students often has emergency grant funds for food, transportation, and basic supplies on top of housing. Ask the same office.

tiles.label: This is overwhelming
tiles.subtitle: CAPS support
tiles.spokenText: Losing housing is a major life event. I want to talk to a counselor.

tiles.label: Serious roommate issue — not just conflict
tiles.spokenText: Serious roommate issue — not just conflict

tiles.label: Is this more than annoyance?
tiles.subtitle: Different paths for different problems
tiles.spokenText: A roommate crisis is different from a normal roommate conflict — like dishes or music. A crisis means your safety, your health, or your ability to function in school is being damaged. The kiosk will help you triage which one you are facing.

tiles.label: I am in immediate danger
tiles.subtitle: Violence / threat right now
tiles.spokenText: If your roommate is being violent or threatening right now, call 911 or campus police immediately. You can also leave the room and go to your RA — they have authority to call for help.

tiles.label: Roommate is harassing me sexually
tiles.subtitle: Title IX applies
tiles.spokenText: If your roommate is making unwanted sexual comments, touching you without consent, watching you change, or pressuring you sexually, this is sexual harassment under Title IX. You have the right to an emergency room change as a supportive measure — without an investigation if you do not want one.

tiles.label: Roommate substance abuse
tiles.subtitle: Endangering me + them
tiles.spokenText: If your roommate is using alcohol or drugs in ways that endanger them or you — passing out, bringing dangerous people to the room, leaving drugs accessible, blacking out frequently — the Resident Director and the CARE team can intervene without you being put at risk. Medical amnesty applies if you call for help in a medical emergency.

tiles.label: Roommate mental health crisis
tiles.subtitle: CARE team + RA
tiles.spokenText: If your roommate is in mental-health crisis — talking about suicide, hurting themselves, severely depressed, having psychotic symptoms — call CAPS for guidance and notify your RA. For active suicide threat, call 988 or 911. You are not betraying them by getting help — you may be saving them.

tiles.label: Roommate is stealing
tiles.subtitle: Conduct + maybe criminal
tiles.spokenText: If your roommate is stealing money or property from you, this is both a code-of-conduct violation and potentially a crime. Document what is missing, what you have seen, and any messages. Report to your RA, the Residence Director, AND consider a campus police report.

tiles.label: They bring people who scare me
tiles.subtitle: Safety concern
tiles.spokenText: If your roommate brings people into the room who make you feel unsafe — through their behavior, things they have said about violence, prior altercations, or just your gut — talk to your Resident Director. You have the right to feel safe in your own room. Room change is a supportive measure, even without proving criminal behavior.

tiles.label: I want to be moved tonight
tiles.subtitle: Emergency room change
tiles.spokenText: Ask your Resident Director or Residence Life for an emergency room change. Many campuses can arrange temporary placement quickly — sometimes within a day — and a permanent reassignment within a few days. Timing depends on availability. You do not have to prove anything to request it; your safety is enough reason to ask.

tiles.subtitle: Yale Health Building · 203-432-2000
tiles.spokenText: Yale SHARE Center (Sexual Harassment and Assault Response & Education). Address: Yale Health Building, Lower Level, 55 Lock Street, New Haven, CT 06511. Phone: 203-432-2000.

tiles.label: I need support too
tiles.spokenText: Living with a roommate in crisis is exhausting. I want a counselor.

tiles.label: Pregnancy is a Title IX-protected category
tiles.spokenText: Pregnancy is a Title IX-protected category

tiles.label: Federal law protects you
tiles.subtitle: Title IX — pregnancy + parenting
tiles.spokenText: Under Title IX, schools that receive federal funds CANNOT discriminate against you based on pregnancy, childbirth, miscarriage, abortion, or related medical conditions. Schools must give you reasonable accommodations — excused absences for medical appointments, deadline extensions when needed, and they cannot exclude you from any educational program. You have these rights regardless of marital status. Specific accommodations like lactation-space access and parental leave vary by school policy and current federal guidance — ask your Title IX coordinator what is available at this school.

tiles.label: Medical emergency
tiles.subtitle: Call 911
tiles.spokenText: If you have a medical emergency related to pregnancy — heavy bleeding, severe pain, signs of pre-eclampsia, or after-birth complications — call 911 immediately.

tiles.label: I'm figuring out what to do
tiles.subtitle: All-options counseling
tiles.spokenText: If you are pregnant and figuring out what you want to do — continue the pregnancy, parent, place for adoption, or abortion — All-Options at 1-888-493-0092 provides free, judgment-free phone support that walks you through all four options without pushing any. The campus health center can also discuss medical options with you confidentially.

tiles.label: Continuing pregnancy — accommodations
tiles.subtitle: Excused absences + extensions
tiles.spokenText: If you are continuing the pregnancy, you can request reasonable accommodations: excused absences for medical appointments and recovery, deadline extensions, modified attendance policies, larger desks, parking near classrooms. After birth, you can request access to private space for lactation — what the school provides specifically varies by current federal guidance and school policy, so ask the Title IX coordinator. Submit your request to the Title IX coordinator or the Disability Services office — both routes work.

tiles.label: Abortion access
tiles.subtitle: CT is a protective state
tiles.spokenText: In Connecticut, abortion is legal. The campus health center can refer you, or you can contact Planned Parenthood at 1-800-230-7526 directly. Connecticut Public Act 22-19 — the shield law — protects providers and patients in Connecticut from certain out-of-state legal actions related to lawful reproductive healthcare. Specific availability of medication abortion and in-clinic procedures depends on gestational age and on the specific clinic — ask Planned Parenthood or the campus health center for current options. Many clinics offer sliding-scale fees; ask when you call.

tiles.label: Miscarriage / pregnancy loss
tiles.subtitle: Time off + grief support
tiles.spokenText: Pregnancy loss is covered under the same Title IX protections — including excused absences for medical care and emotional recovery. Many people need a week or more. The Dean of Students can excuse classes; the counseling center has grief support specifically for pregnancy loss.

tiles.label: After birth — lactation + parenting
tiles.subtitle: Time + space + childcare
tiles.spokenText: After childbirth, ask the Title IX coordinator about lactation accommodations on campus — many schools provide private non-bathroom lactation space and reasonable break time for lactation, though specifics vary by school. Some campuses have childcare centers with student priority; some have parent-student groups. Ask the Title IX coordinator for the full list of resources.

tiles.label: Returning to school post-birth
tiles.subtitle: Catch-up plan
tiles.spokenText: Coming back from maternity leave is hard. The Dean of Students office can help you build a catch-up plan: incomplete grades, modified course loads, deferred deadlines, summer-term options. Many faculty are willing to work with you — but the dean coordinates so you do not have to negotiate with each.

tiles.label: Family / student-parent housing
tiles.subtitle: Different from dorms
tiles.spokenText: Most campuses have student-family housing for students with children — usually apartment-style, separate from the dorms. If your campus does not, the Dean of Students can advise on off-campus partner buildings and help with rental security deposits via emergency grants.

tiles.label: Financial aid + dependent
tiles.subtitle: You can claim them
tiles.spokenText: Adding a dependent child changes your FAFSA — your expected family contribution drops, your aid usually increases. File an updated FAFSA promptly after birth. Financial aid can also help with the additional costs of textbooks and supplies when your dependent count changes.

tiles.label: Office of Institutional Equity and Accessibility (OIEA) — University Title IX Office
tiles.subtitle: 82-90 Wall Street · 203-432-6854
tiles.spokenText: Office of Institutional Equity and Accessibility (OIEA) — University Title IX Office. Address: 82-90 Wall Street, 4th Floor, New Haven, CT 06511. Phone: 203-432-6854.

tiles.subtitle: 55 Lock Street · 203-432-0246
tiles.spokenText: Yale Health Center. Address: 55 Lock Street, New Haven, CT 06520. Phone: 203-432-0246.

tiles.subtitle: 1 Hillhouse Avenue · 203-432-2900
tiles.spokenText: Office of the Dean of Yale College. Address: 1 Hillhouse Avenue, New Haven, CT 06511. Phone: 203-432-2900.

tiles.label: All-Options helpline
tiles.spokenText: All-Options helpline at 1-888-493-0092 provides free, judgment-free pregnancy options counseling. They will not push any direction. Available in English and Spanish.

tiles.label: Planned Parenthood
tiles.spokenText: Planned Parenthood at 1-800-230-7526 for medical care including pregnancy testing, prenatal care, abortion care, contraception, and STI testing. Many CT locations.

tiles.label: Records, safety, daily life
tiles.spokenText: Records, safety, daily life

tiles.label: You belong here
tiles.subtitle: Your rights under federal law
tiles.spokenText: You belong here. Title IX protections include gender identity per current federal guidance, and most institutions have campus policies that go further. The kiosk can help you with the practical steps: name changes, pronouns, housing, restrooms, medical care, safety.

tiles.label: I am being threatened / harmed
tiles.subtitle: Safety first
tiles.spokenText: If you are being threatened or attacked because of your gender identity, this is both a campus conduct violation and potentially a hate crime. Call 911 if you are in immediate danger. Otherwise file a bias incident report — campus police if it was physical, bias-incident team if not.

tiles.label: Change my name on records
tiles.subtitle: Registrar + ID + email
tiles.spokenText: Most institutions allow students to set a chosen / preferred name across systems — class rosters, email, ID card, dining swipe, library — without legal documentation. Some require a separate process for the legal name on transcript. The registrar has the form. If your name is not legally changed yet, the chosen-name policy still applies to nearly everything except the transcript and federal-aid records.

tiles.label: Yale University Registrar's Office
tiles.subtitle: 246 Church Street · 203-432-2330
tiles.spokenText: Yale University Registrar's Office. Address: 246 Church Street, 3rd Floor, New Haven, CT 06520. Phone: 203-432-2330.

tiles.label: Pronouns in class roster
tiles.subtitle: Student portal usually
tiles.spokenText: Many institutions let you set your pronouns in the student portal so they appear on class rosters. Faculty are usually expected to use the pronouns you set. If a professor refuses, that may be a bias incident or a Title IX issue — keep documentation and file a report.

tiles.label: Faculty/staff is dead-naming me
tiles.subtitle: It is not OK — document
tiles.spokenText: If a faculty or staff member is repeatedly calling you by your old name or wrong pronouns after being corrected, that is dead-naming and it is a form of harassment. Document the incidents: date, what was said, who else heard. File a bias-incident report. The Office for Equity / DEI will follow up. You can also escalate through the Dean of Students.

tiles.label: Restroom access
tiles.subtitle: Map of all-gender restrooms
tiles.spokenText: Most campuses have a published map of all-gender / gender-inclusive restrooms across academic buildings. Ask the LGBTQ+ Center or check the campus accessibility map. Federal Title IX guidance has gone back and forth on requiring all-gender bathrooms — most CT institutions have them as campus policy regardless of federal status.

tiles.label: Gender-inclusive housing
tiles.subtitle: Residence Life
tiles.spokenText: Most institutions offer gender-inclusive housing — rooms or suites where roommates of any gender can live together. Some have specific LGBTQ+ themed living-learning communities. Apply through Residence Life; ask for the gender-inclusive option.

tiles.label: Gender-affirming medical care
tiles.subtitle: On + off campus
tiles.spokenText: Connecticut is a shield-law state — gender-affirming care is protected from out-of-state legal threats. Many campus health centers offer hormone-therapy management, hormone-bridging if you are between providers, and referrals to gender-affirming surgical care. If yours does not, the Yale Gender Health Program in New Haven and Planned Parenthood are both options.

tiles.label: Identity-affirming counseling
tiles.subtitle: Specifically trained
tiles.spokenText: I want a counselor who is specifically trained in supporting trans and non-binary clients.

tiles.label: Trans Lifeline
tiles.spokenText: Trans Lifeline at 877-565-8860 — peer support by and for trans and non-binary people. They run a 24/7 hotline staffed entirely by trans people.

tiles.label: The Trevor Project (under 25)
tiles.spokenText: The Trevor Project — for LGBTQ+ young people under 25. Phone 866-488-7386, or text START to 678-678.

tiles.label: Trans Equality (NCTE)
tiles.subtitle: Legal + policy info
tiles.spokenText: National Center for Transgender Equality — transequality.org — has detailed guides on legal name change, gender-marker updates on IDs and passports, and your rights as a trans student.

tiles.label: Visa-status emergency — fast clock
tiles.spokenText: Visa-status emergency — fast clock

tiles.label: This is time-sensitive
tiles.subtitle: Talk to ISSS TODAY
tiles.spokenText: SEVIS termination means the government may consider you out of legal student status. This can lead to losing your F-1 or J-1 status, losing your work authorization, and eventually deportation if not resolved. There ARE restoration paths but they have tight clocks. The most important thing right now: contact your International Student Services office TODAY, before doing anything else.

tiles.label: Office of International Students & Scholars (OISS)
tiles.subtitle: 421 Temple Street · 203-432-7166
tiles.spokenText: Office of International Students & Scholars (OISS). Address: 421 Temple Street, New Haven, CT 06511. Phone: 203-432-7166.

tiles.label: Why did this happen?
tiles.subtitle: Common reasons
tiles.spokenText: Common reasons for SEVIS termination: dropping below full-time enrollment without authorization, unauthorized employment, not reporting an address change, suspension for over five months, failing to make academic progress, gaps in enrollment between terms. Each has a different recovery path. Your DSO — designated school official — will figure out which applies.

tiles.label: Reinstatement path
tiles.subtitle: Form I-539
tiles.spokenText: If you are still in the United States, you can apply for reinstatement to F-1 status by filing Form I-539 with USCIS. Filing fee is around 470 dollars. Processing takes weeks to months. While the application is pending, you can usually stay in the US but you cannot work. Your DSO will help you build the application. Eligibility narrowly requires that the violation was due to circumstances beyond your control OR caused by school error.

tiles.label: Travel + re-entry path
tiles.subtitle: New initial I-20
tiles.spokenText: An alternative to reinstatement is to leave the United States and re-enter on a new initial I-20 from your school. This involves applying for a new F-1 visa at a US embassy abroad, which may be denied for various reasons. The advantage is that it does not require USCIS approval. The disadvantage is the visa-application risk. Your DSO can help you weigh both paths.

tiles.label: Termination was school error
tiles.subtitle: Easier fix
tiles.spokenText: If the SEVIS record was terminated by mistake — say, the registrar reported you as withdrawn when you were not — the DSO can request a SEVIS data fix from SEVP. This is much faster and cheaper than reinstatement. Bring documentation showing you were enrolled.

tiles.label: While pending — do these now
tiles.subtitle: Protect your record
tiles.spokenText: While reinstatement is pending: do NOT work, on or off campus. Do NOT travel internationally. Stay enrolled. Keep all your paperwork — passport, I-20, I-94. Document any work you have NOT done (in case immigration asks).

tiles.label: Get an immigration attorney
tiles.subtitle: AILA + low-cost clinics
tiles.spokenText: For complex cases, hire an immigration attorney. The American Immigration Lawyers Association — AILA — at aila.org has a directory. Most CT law schools have immigration clinics that offer free or low-cost help. Connecticut Legal Services may be able to refer you.

tiles.label: ICE detained me or family
tiles.subtitle: Different urgency
tiles.spokenText: If you or a family member has been detained by ICE, this requires immediate legal help. CT has an ICE detainee hotline through the New Haven Legal Assistance Association. The Connecticut Immigrant Rights Alliance — CIRA — also coordinates emergency response. Do NOT sign anything without an attorney.

tiles.label: This is overwhelming
tiles.subtitle: Counselor — your DSO knows
tiles.spokenText: Status uncertainty is one of the most stressful things in college. I want to talk to a counselor.

tiles.label: Federal aid suspended — winnable with appeal
tiles.spokenText: Federal aid suspended — winnable with appeal

tiles.label: SAP appeals usually win
tiles.subtitle: But the deadline is tight
tiles.spokenText: If you have been notified that you lost federal financial aid because of Satisfactory Academic Progress — SAP — the appeal process exists exactly for this reason. A complete, well-documented appeal that names a recognized circumstance and shows a plan to regain SAP has the strongest chance. The deadline is usually short — often within fourteen days of the notice, though it varies by school. Start TODAY and ask financial aid for the exact deadline at this school.

tiles.label: Read the notice
tiles.subtitle: Which standard failed?
tiles.spokenText: Read your SAP-failure notice carefully. Federal SAP has three standards: GPA (usually 2.0 minimum), pace of completion (usually 67 percent of attempted credits earned), and maximum time frame (usually 150 percent of program length). The notice should tell you which one you failed. Different standards have different appeal arguments.

tiles.label: Document your specific circumstance
tiles.subtitle: 34 CFR 668.34
tiles.spokenText: Federal regulation 34 CFR section 668-point-34 names specific bases for an SAP appeal: the death of a relative of the student, an injury or illness of the student, or other special circumstances. Document yours: medical records, death certificate, mental-health provider letter, police report for DV, financial documentation. The school sets its own appeal procedures within this framework.

tiles.label: Gather documentation
tiles.subtitle: Doctor / dean / counselor letters
tiles.spokenText: Gather: medical records or doctor letter for illness, death certificate for bereavement, counselor or therapist letter for mental health, police report for DV, FAFSA or other docs for financial hardship, advisor letter explaining the academic struggle, your own statement. The more concrete the documentation, the stronger the appeal.

tiles.label: Plan to get back to SAP
tiles.subtitle: Required for appeal
tiles.spokenText: Federal regulations require your appeal to include a plan to regain SAP — usually within one to three terms. Work with your academic advisor to build a realistic plan: which classes, what GPA per term, what supports you will use. Include this in your written appeal. Show that you have a path forward, not just an explanation of the past.

tiles.label: If appeal granted — probation
tiles.subtitle: One-term grace
tiles.spokenText: If your appeal is granted, you will usually be placed on Financial Aid Probation for one term. During probation you keep your aid but must meet the academic plan. Hit the plan and you go back to good standing. Miss it and you lose aid again.

tiles.label: Appeal denied — second appeal?
tiles.subtitle: Limited but possible
tiles.spokenText: If your appeal is denied, ask the financial aid office: is there a second-level appeal? Can I submit additional documentation? Some schools allow a second appeal with new evidence. If not, you may be able to pay out of pocket for one term, raise your GPA / completion rate, and regain SAP for the following term without aid.

tiles.label: Can't pay — emergency funds
tiles.subtitle: Bridge to next term
tiles.spokenText: If your appeal was denied and you cannot pay out of pocket for the next term, the Dean of Students office often has emergency grants. Some institutions have institutional aid that is separate from federal aid. Outside scholarships are another bridge.

tiles.label: Medical reason — also drop / withdraw
tiles.subtitle: Coordinate paths
tiles.spokenText: If your SAP failure was due to medical reasons, also consider whether a medical withdrawal from the failed term — backdated through the dean of students — could be cleaner than the appeal. Sometimes a medical withdrawal followed by re-enrollment in a future term has better aid implications than an appeal-with-probation.

tiles.label: Veteran benefits + SAP
tiles.subtitle: Different rules
tiles.spokenText: If you receive Post-9/11 GI Bill or other veteran benefits, SAP rules and appeals are slightly different — VA has its own. Talk to your campus Veterans Services office in addition to financial aid.

tiles.label: Routine housing requests
tiles.spokenText: Routine housing requests

tiles.label: Roommate conflict (not crisis)
tiles.subtitle: Dishes · sleep · guests
tiles.spokenText: Routine roommate conflict — like dishes, sleep schedules, music, guests. The first step is usually a roommate-agreement conversation, often mediated by your Resident Assistant. The RA can also help you draft a roommate agreement document, which makes future conflicts easier to resolve. If conflict escalates beyond routine, the Resident Director gets involved.

tiles.label: Roommate crisis (sexual / substance / MH)
tiles.subtitle: Different path
tiles.spokenText: If the roommate situation is more serious — sexual harassment, substance abuse endangering me, mental-health crisis — the kiosk has a separate roommate-crisis path with safer options.

tiles.label: Maintenance request
tiles.subtitle: Heat · plumbing · pests
tiles.spokenText: For maintenance issues in your dorm room — heat / cooling, plumbing leak, broken window, pest sighting — submit a maintenance request through the residence-life portal. For urgent issues (no heat in winter, water leak, mold) call the residence-life on-call line for same-day response.

tiles.label: Locked out
tiles.subtitle: RA / RD on-call
tiles.spokenText: For dorm lockout, contact your Resident Assistant first. They can let you in or page the on-call Resident Director. Many campuses charge a small fee for after-hours lockouts; the first one is often waived.

tiles.label: Lost or stolen key / card
tiles.subtitle: Replace at One Card
tiles.spokenText: For lost or stolen room key or campus ID card, go to the OneCard or campus ID office to replace it. Some campuses also let you self-suspend a lost ID online to prevent unauthorized use until you can get to the office. Bring photo ID.

tiles.label: Move-in / move-out logistics
tiles.subtitle: Dates · keys · check-out
tiles.spokenText: For move-in or move-out — assigned dates, key pickup/return procedure, room inspection process, mail forwarding, storage between semesters — your Residence Life office has the official move-in and move-out guides.

tiles.label: Summer storage
tiles.subtitle: On + off campus options
tiles.spokenText: For storing belongings between semesters: some campuses provide free on-campus storage in unused spaces, especially for international students who cannot fly with everything. Storage Squad and Dorm Room Movers are common off-campus options used by college students nationwide. Ask Residence Life for the campus storage policy.

tiles.label: Emotional support animal
tiles.subtitle: ESA accommodation
tiles.spokenText: For an emotional support animal in a dorm: this is a disability accommodation request. Many campuses route ESA requests through Disability Services, but some use Housing or a housing portal first — check your campus housing portal or Disability Services to find out which applies. You will need a letter from a treating mental-health provider. Submit early — the process takes a few weeks. ESAs are not service animals; the rules and rights are different.

tiles.spokenText: Office of the Dean of Yale College. Address: 1 Hillhouse Avenue, New Haven, CT 06511. Phone: 203-432-2900.
