tiles.label: Connecticut-specific resources
tiles.spokenText: Connecticut-specific resources

tiles.label: You have a path in CT
tiles.subtitle: In-state tuition + state aid
tiles.spokenText: Connecticut is one of about 24 states that extends in-state tuition to undocumented students who meet specific criteria — typically graduating from a CT high school after attending for a set number of years. Connecticut Public Act 11-43 (2011) created the in-state tuition path, with later acts (including PA 15-82) refining the criteria. Connecticut Public Act 18-2 opened institutional financial aid at public CT institutions for certain undocumented students, subject to state-law criteria. Eligibility depends on the specific statute — verify with admissions or financial aid. You are not alone; there is a community here.

tiles.label: WHO to disclose to
tiles.subtitle: Be careful
tiles.spokenText: Important: be careful who knows your status. Confidential resources — campus counselors in their treatment role, designated victim advocates, attorneys — generally must keep what you share private (subject to standard legal/safety exceptions). Mandatory reporters do NOT keep disclosures private. Many CT institutions treat undocumented-student-program coordinators and specifically-trained financial aid officers as confidential or limited-disclosure for this purpose — but it varies by school. Confirm with them directly before disclosing: ask "Is what I tell you confidential, and if so, what exceptions apply?" Random staff members or peers usually are not bound by confidentiality.

tiles.label: FERPA + immigration
tiles.subtitle: School records are protected
tiles.spokenText: Your enrollment records at the school are protected by FERPA — Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act. Schools generally may not disclose FERPA-protected records without consent unless a FERPA exception applies, including compliance with a lawfully issued subpoena or judicial order. An informal request from a federal agent without a subpoena or court order generally does not require disclosure. Many CT institutions have policies that clarify their FERPA-compliance practices — ask the registrar for the policy in writing.

tiles.label: In-state tuition in CT
tiles.subtitle: PA 11-43 / PA 18-2
tiles.spokenText: Connecticut Public Act 11-43 (2011), with later amendments including PA 15-82, generally extends in-state tuition rates to undocumented students who meet specific criteria — typically attending a CT high school for a set number of years, graduating from a CT high school, and signing an affidavit. The exact criteria depend on the current statute; verify with admissions before assuming eligibility. Apply through admissions or the registrar; do not be afraid to ask. The savings can be tens of thousands of dollars.

tiles.label: CT state institutional aid
tiles.subtitle: PA 18-2
tiles.spokenText: Connecticut Public Act 18-2 (2018) opened access to state institutional aid at public CT institutions for certain undocumented students, subject to state-law criteria. You generally cannot receive federal financial aid (no FAFSA), but state institutional aid AND outside scholarships fill significant gaps. Talk to a financial aid officer who has been trained in undocumented-student support.

tiles.label: DACA renewal
tiles.subtitle: Every 2 years
tiles.spokenText: DACA — Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals — must be renewed every two years. Start the renewal process 150 days before expiration. The fee changes; CHIRLA and other immigration legal nonprofits offer free help with renewals. USCIS continues to accept both initial and renewal DACA filings, but as of mid-2026 currently only approves renewals — initial applications are accepted but held pending. Talk to an immigration attorney before filing initial.

tiles.label: TheDream.US scholarship
tiles.subtitle: For DACA + TPS students
tiles.spokenText: TheDream.US is the largest scholarship program for DACA and TPS students. Current National Scholarship awards are up to about $16,500 for an associate degree or $33,000 for a bachelor degree at participating National Partner Colleges. Verify current award amounts at thedream.us. Many CT institutions are partners.

tiles.label: Other scholarships — no status required
tiles.subtitle: HSF, MALDEF, etc.
tiles.spokenText: Many scholarships do not require immigration status verification — Hispanic Scholarship Fund, MALDEF, Golden Door Scholars, Educators for Fair Consideration. The campus financial aid office and the undocumented-student program coordinator can connect you with the full list.

tiles.label: Free legal help
tiles.subtitle: CIRA + IRIS + clinics
tiles.spokenText: Free immigration legal help in CT — Connecticut Immigrant Rights Alliance (CIRA), Integrated Refugee and Immigrant Services (IRIS) in New Haven, Yale Law School and UConn Law School immigration clinics. The Connecticut Bar Association has a referral service. For urgent matters, AILA (American Immigration Lawyers Association) has a directory.

tiles.label: If ICE comes to campus
tiles.subtitle: Your rights
tiles.spokenText: If ICE or a federal agent approaches you or comes to campus: you have the right to remain silent. You can say "I am exercising my right to remain silent." You can ask "Am I free to leave?" — if yes, walk away calmly. Do not sign anything before legal review. Ask to speak with a lawyer (note: in immigration proceedings, attorney representation is at no cost to the government — you must pay your own or work with free legal nonprofits). Do not lie or run. Some CT campuses publish welcoming-campus or privacy policies, but legal "sanctuary" status varies — do not assume your campus has formal legal protection. Contact the Dean of Students or an immigration attorney immediately. Save the legal-help phone numbers from this kiosk in your phone NOW.

tiles.spokenText: United We Dream MigraWatch hotline — 1-844-363-1423 — connects with rapid-response support for ICE encounters. Save this number.

tiles.label: Mental health (confidential)
tiles.subtitle: CAPS does not report status
tiles.spokenText: Campus counseling — CAPS — is generally confidential in their treatment role, subject to standard legal and safety exceptions (such as imminent danger or mandated reporting of child or elder abuse). Counselors are not immigration officers and the purpose of treatment is your wellbeing, not status verification. Many counselors are specifically trained in undocumented-student mental-health.
